items.planLine: CLOSE-UP — Sarah alone — Sarah bends over the honour roll at her desk, brush in hand, lettering Noah's name onto the scroll after seeing the silver stars on him that morning — Noah's name is now on the honour roll
items.arc:
1. On the Friday evening before the first cold Saturday of autumn, Noah lifts the silver-star cape off its peg in the back corridor of the Heldenwache, because tomorrow he walks his first cold patrol and he wants to walk in front the way Hans once did; Emma watches through the gap in the curtain and says, "That one is Hans's. Hang it back before he looks for it." — but Noah is stubborn and folds it into his bag.
2. On Saturday morning Sarah looks up from the honour roll she has been lettering for weeks for the evening naming of Lumoria's youngest cape-bearer and asks Noah who gave him a cape with silver stars; Daniel is already in the doorway calling the patrol out into the wind, so nobody waits long, and when Sarah says, "Then Hans has chosen you," Noah does not correct her, therefore his ears go hot and stay hot.
3. At the Kastanienplatz the wind brings the chestnut leaves down in a brown wall and the smallest children lose the path, so Noah walks in front of them and brings every one of them to their door; Daniel praises him there, in front of all the families, and says the walk was the bravest thing he has seen this year, therefore that praise is finished before noon — but Noah is proud of his feet and sick about his shoulders.
4. At noon Hans comes to fetch his cape, because he has led the lantern walk in it for forty autumns and tonight is the last walk he will lead; he finds the peg empty, he finds the silver stars on Noah, and he says quietly that he will not start the walk without it.
5. Sarah asks Hans to lead in a plain cape so that her ceremony can begin on time, but Hans will not, therefore the children's lanterns stay unlit on the wall; Emma has waited a whole year to carry a light through the dark park and she is afraid of the dark without one, so she cries, and when Noah asks her to say the wind took the cape she says she will not say a thing that is not true.
6. Before dusk Noah carries the cape back to hang it up, but Hans is sitting in the corridor under the empty peg, so Noah turns and runs, and the cape drags through the soaked leaves along the tower gutter until the silver star is stiff with brown mud; his plan is gone, therefore he pushes the heavy wet bundle under his jacket and keeps it there.
7. Emma goes to Hans and tells him plainly that she knows where the cape is, and she asks him to wait until the lantern lighting so that Noah can say it himself; Hans agrees to wait exactly that long and then tells Noah what his sister did, therefore Noah, who cannot bear to be caught losing, does not speak to Emma for the rest of the afternoon and Emma stands by the lantern wall alone.
8. At dusk in the square Sarah lifts the honour roll to name the youngest cape-bearer, Hans stands with his lantern unlit, Emma stands in the dark with empty hands, and Sarah reads out Noah's name; Noah steps forward with the muddy bundle under his jacket, and he is frightened.
9. Noah says out loud that nobody gave him the cape and that he took it off Hans's peg on Friday, then he pulls it out and lays it muddy in Hans's hands; Sarah strikes his name from the roll where everyone can see it and says the naming will wait until there is a giver, Hans says Noah will brush and dry that cape with him every Saturday until spring, and Noah turns to Emma first and tells her she was right and that he is sorry.
10. Hans lights his lantern and begins his last walk in the mud-starred cape, therefore the children's lanterns come off the wall at last; Emma carries her own light out in front through the dark park without reaching for a hand, and Noah walks beside her with no cape at all and says the evening feels lighter than the morning did.

Challenges taken:
1. Noah: following rules — he takes what was not given.
2. Noah: controlling feelings, hating to lose — he cannot say it out loud.
3. Emma: refusing to lie though she loves her brother.
4. Emma: fear of the dark without a light.

items.planLine: close-up — Julian — Julian sits alone on the bank of the fast stream, arms wrapped around his knees, the rushing water filling the frame beside him — Julian is too afraid to move forward without help
items.arc:
Third invented name (allowance is two): Gian and Vroni are the commission's two guardians and cannot be one figure — Gian holds the refusal, Vroni holds the reason, and one ibex doing both turns the opposition into a rule instead of a person; Flügi is the commissioned dragon himself and takes his name from Julian on the page.

Commission's three paths: the four stay together on one path, because Nia can hold only one warm trail and Julian will not walk anywhere without Levin.

1. It is summer. Levin and Julian ride their Velos out of Zurich, past the Grossmünster and over the Limmat bridge. Levin wants to find a real dragon cave, so they take the forest road up the mountain with the tall tower.
2. High up, a blue chip lies in front of a dark hole in the rock. Levin picks it up. It is warm in his hand. Julian stays close behind his brother, because the hole is dark.
3. A dragon squeezes out of the hole and sits down slowly. One patch on his wing is bare, and the patch is much bigger than the chip. He says he cannot lift himself off the ground. Levin is glad, not scared.
4. Julian gives him the name Flügi. Flügi shows scratches he cut into his cave wall. A storm broke his wing scale in two; the corner fell by his door, and two ibexes, Gian and Vroni, carried the big half up to the Felsenegg.
5. Flügi called after them, but they kept it. With one wing dragging he cannot climb the steep path. Levin says out loud that they will bring the big half back before the sun goes behind the trees, so Flügi can fly home to his family tonight.
6. Nia comes running out of the trees and pushes her nose into Levin's warm hand. Max talks fast: they were riding the same forest road when Nia smelled something warm and ran off. Kiaan looks at the bare wing and says he is coming too.
7. Kiaan reads the little sign at the path aloud: "Felsenegg — one hour." The four climb. Soon the path stops at a stream. The bridge is gone, and red stones from a rockfall lie all over the bank.
8. Julian sits down and will not go on, because the water is fast. Then he asks Levin for his hand. Levin goes first and pulls him over the wet beams. Both are wet to the knees.
9. The crossing cost them time, and the sun stands lower now. Higher up a red boulder from the same slide blocks the path. Max shoves, Nia digs, Kiaan pulls, and Levin levers the stone aside with a branch. The earth under it is dark and wet, so Levin keeps the branch.
10. On the summit Gian and Vroni step out from behind the stone cairn. The big blue scale lies in a dry stone trough. Vroni licks two drops of water off the warm scale. Gian stands in front of the trough and does not move.
11. Kiaan holds the little chip against the big scale. The broken edges fit together. Levin says the scale belongs to Flügi and asks for it back. Gian says one word: "Nein."
12. Julian offers his red ball. Gian pushes it away with his nose and says: "Wasser." Vroni points at the crack beside the trough, packed tight with red gravel. The slide buried their spring, so the drops on the warm scale are all they get.
13. The light is going, so Vroni lets them try the crack one single time. All four scrape at the gravel with their hands until their fingers hurt. Only the loose stones come out. No water comes.
14. Gian pushes the scale deep into the trough. He lies down in front of it and turns his head away. Julian cries. Levin sits in the grass and has no idea left.
15. Then Levin remembers the dark wet earth under the red boulder. He says the water is stuck under the stones, deeper than their hands reached. He rams his branch into the crack and heaves. Water shoots out and runs into a hollow beside the trough.
16. Gian and Vroni get up and drink. Julian walks to Gian all by himself and holds out both hands. Gian lifts the scale out of the trough and lays it in them.
17. Down at the cave the scale slides into the bare patch. The wing shines silver-blue. Flügi lifts off the grass. Then he kneels and lets all four climb onto his back.
18. Flügi carries them in one wide circle over Zurich, past the tall tower and over the lake. Then he sets them by their Velos and flies home over the water. Julian pushes off first and says he is proud, because he asked the big ibex all by himself.

Challenges taken:
1. The washed-out stream where the bridge is gone.
2. The red boulder from the same slide.
3. Gian and Vroni's refusal to hand the scale over.
4. The spring buried under packed red gravel.

items.arc:
1. It is high summer in the harbour of Cala Nera, where the «Goldene Möwe» and the «Schwarze Distel» lie in neighbouring berths, and Fiona lifts a treasure map out of her grandmother's sea chest and tells Lorena she means to fetch the treasure no one has reached in two generations.
2. The old cloth crumbles at every fold, therefore Fiona copies it onto sailcloth with the charcoal stub from her belt, reading the last marks aloud as she draws them, and she starts the copy over twice because one line runs crooked.
3. Lorena watches the water and says, "Wind turns at noon. Copy's good enough. Sail now." — but Fiona keeps drawing, because she is happy only when a chart is clean.
4. From the next berth Rossa sees the twin map in Fiona's hands, holds up her own copy out of her own grandmother's chest and shouts, "My ship is the faster one, so whoever lands last sails home with empty hands!" — Fiona is angry at herself, therefore she orders the lines cast off at last.
5. Sarah is to free the mainsail, but she talks so long about the size of Rossa's hat that the sail stays furled until the «Schwarze Distel» is already out of the bay, while Facundo hauls the last water cask aboard and stacks the casks crosswise, because he never stows anything straight.
6. In the night a cask slides out of the crooked stack and splits, therefore half the drinking water runs into the bilge; Saira calls down, "Harbour! No — press on! No, wait —" and cannot choose, so Fiona holds the course and halves the rations, and the crew sails two thirsty days.
7. On the third evening they reach the island Mandelstein and see the «Schwarze Distel» already at anchor, therefore Fiona believes everything is lost — but footprints run from the water up a dry riverbed, so the crew follows them.
8. The footprints end at a cliff where a thin waterfall still runs from a spring above; Fiona climbs the wet rock and slips back down, and the copy in her belt is soaked and tears, so the piece with the cistern mark washes away.
9. At dawn they climb a wrong gully and lose the whole morning, therefore Fiona is ashamed that her own slip cost the time — but Saira scrambles onto a ledge, shouts "Almond tree, up there, I see the crown!", and points above the fall.
10. Fiona tears a rag from the sailcloth backing and redraws the last stretch from the marks she read aloud in harbour; the lines come out crooked, and she keeps them anyway, though it hurts her to leave them.
11. Behind the falling water lies a dry band of rock, so Facundo lifts Saira onto it and the crew climbs to the almond tree, where an old cistern stands with a snapped rope hanging over the rim, Rossa below beside the chest, alone, because she let no one else touch it first and ordered her crew to stay aboard.
12. Fiona lowers the boat's lead-line, but Rossa calls up, "Keep it — whoever pulls me out will say the chest is theirs," and Lorena says flatly that the line is too short in any case.
13. Facundo runs down to the beach and comes back with the mainsail lines, says loudly, "Then we crawl home without a mainsail," and plaits them onto the lead-line; Rossa knots the rope around the chest herself, Saira and Sarah haul it up, and Rossa climbs out after it on her own hands.
14. Rossa takes the chest as the first to land and drags it up the steep path, but it slides back down twice in front of everyone, therefore Fiona offers Facundo's arms for half the silver, and Rossa grips the offered handle.
15. On the beach they open the lid: silver coins lie inside, and under them a picture of two young captains — Fiona's grandmother and Rossa's — who hid the treasure together and each kept a copy of the map, so Rossa counts out half although she landed first, and rows it to her ship.
16. The «Goldene Möwe» crawls home to Cala Nera under a bare mast with Sarah retelling the cistern the whole way, and Fiona sits at the tiller holding her crooked rag map and is proud of it.

Challenges taken:
1. Perfect copy versus the noon wind — the lead is lost.
2. Split cask, half water, no harbour on the course.
3. Torn map, wrong gully, a lost morning.
4. Rossa in the cistern, the line too short, the chest too heavy.

items.planLine: close-up — Max's face, chin lifted, mouth open mid-shout, one arm flung out — Max shouts that the scale belongs to a dragon — Max's outburst is the last persuasion tried; it has not worked
items.arc:
1. On a summer morning Levin and Julian stand with their bikes on the Rathausbrücke over the Limmat, and Levin shows Julian the new lamp on his handlebar, because he does not like the dark and the lamp is the best thing he owns; Julian puts a roll in his pocket; Mama says one thing: be back at this bridge before the streetlights come on, she will wait here.
2. They ride out of the city and push their bikes up the Farnberg, where the path ends at a cave mouth; Levin leans his bike on a rock and leaves the lamp clipped to the handlebar, because Julian reminds him that he forgets whatever he carries.
3. In the moss at the cave mouth Levin picks up a small golden scale, and he says it is warm, warmer than a stone in the sun; he lets Julian feel it too.
4. A dragon comes out of the cave, so big that his shoulder fills the entrance, and there is a gap in his right wing; Julian is frightened and hides behind Levin, but then he peeks out and says hello, and the dragon says his name is Fenno and that the little scale chipped off his big wing scale when it hit the ground this morning.
5. Nia comes up the path with Max and Kiaan pushing their bikes behind her; Max says she turned off the lake road and would not stop for anything, and Kiaan kneels down and whispers that until today he had only read about dragons.
6. Fenno tells all four that a Bergmännli called Nolo snatched the big scale here at his own cave mouth and carried it up the Zwirbelspitz, therefore he cannot fly home to his family tonight; he says he is ashamed to ask children.
7. Levin says it out loud: "We bring the scale back before the streetlights come on, and nobody walks alone"; at the fork Kiaan reads Zwirbelspitz on the signpost while Nia pulls up the middle path, but the ridge is long, so the climb eats the whole afternoon.
8. On the summit Nolo sits in a hole between the rocks, a small grey Bergmännli with the big scale under his chin, and he says he found it, therefore it is his; his lantern stone cracked years ago, so this is the brightest thing left on his mountain.
9. Kiaan asks him politely and Julian holds out his roll, but Max shouts that the scale belongs to a dragon; therefore Nolo drags a stone slab over his hole and says nothing more, and Levin has no idea left.
10. Down at the cave Fenno lies flat and says they should go home, but Levin looks at the lamp on his handlebar and says Nolo does not want gold, he wants light; therefore Levin unclips the lamp, although it is the only thing that would get him home in the dark.
11. They climb the Zwirbelspitz a second time, their legs burn, and the sun goes down behind the Uetliberg; Levin knocks on the slab and clicks the lamp on.
12. Nolo grabs for the lamp, but Levin sets it down on the stone, steps back out of reach and says nobody will take it back; therefore Nolo clicks the button twice and pushes the big scale across to him.
13. Nolo follows them down the slope, because he says they will grab his lamp back as soon as it is properly dark; on the loose scree Levin stumbles, therefore the big scale slips out of his hands and slides deep between the stones.
14. Nolo says lost is lost, tomorrow he will dig it out and it will be his again, therefore he will not shine his lamp for boys who want it back; Levin says straight out that he dropped it and that it is his fault, and nobody shouts at him, but Julian cries and Levin is afraid of the dark.
15. Then Levin remembers how the little scale felt in his hand in the morning, so he crawls over the scree and lays both palms on stone after stone until one stone is warm; he pulls the big scale out from under it, and Nolo stands three steps away and says nothing.
16. At the cave Levin presses the scale into the gap and Fenno's wing closes and lifts him off the ground; Nolo watches from the cave mouth, then clicks his lamp on and climbs down into his tunnels with it.
17. Fenno kneels so the four boys and Nia can climb on, therefore they ride once over Zurich, past the towers of the Grossmünster and along the Limmat, and he sets them down at the Rathausbrücke, where Mama is waiting under the lit streetlights and Levin tells her at once that he is late and that his lamp is gone for good.
18. Mama pulls him close and says she saw a big shadow cross the water; Fenno lifts off and turns toward his own mountains, and the four boys ride home together through the dark streets, and Levin is not afraid of the dark, because he found the scale in it with his own hands.

Challenges taken:
1. Nolo refuses and shuts himself in.
2. Levin gives up his lamp and climbs twice.
3. The scale is lost in the dark, and the light is Nolo's.
4. Coming home late with no light.

items.planLine: close-up — Facundo alone, facing forward, fists at his sides — he says out loud that it is his fault; Fiona stands small in the background, head bowed — the loss is named and felt; the question of turning back is open
items.arc:
1. On a windy autumn afternoon Fiona sits at her kitchen table in Zurich and copies a torn old chart onto clean paper, because the chest that chart shows is on no map any more; she tells Sarah that they must reach it before next week's storms shut the sea. Sarah leans over her shoulder and names the marks she has heard Fiona describe a hundred times: three rocks, a black cove, a shelf of sand. Fiona says the rest is only her memory, therefore the map has to be perfect. Rain stands on the window above the towers of the Grossmünster.

2. Saira and Lorena come up the stairs with the costume bag. Lorena says, short and flat, that she is not going home without that chest, so she pulls her boots on first. Saira cannot choose between two hats, therefore she wears both. Facundo arrives last and drops his sword, his belt and his wet boots in the middle of the kitchen floor.

3. Fiona spreads the map wide on the table. The window bangs open, the autumn wind pours through, and in the next moment all five stand in pirate coats on the deck of the Sturmfeder with the grey sea rolling under them. Lorena points ahead at a rusty chain lying across a harbour mouth and says the name: Krummhafen, the town that lets no stranger through.

4. A black rowing boat comes out from under the chain. Hafenmeisterin Malva Grimm rows twice around the ship and looks far longer at the map in Fiona's hands than at the crew, therefore Fiona holds it flat against her coat. Malva says she has hunted that same chest for eleven years with a chart torn in half, so she will lift the chain this minute if Fiona hands the map down. Fiona feels her stomach go cold, but she says no.

5. Malva does not argue. She says the chain lifts only for a crew this town owes something, then she rows the five to the quay herself, because she is sure they will fail and come back to her offer. On the quay the dockworkers crowd round and shout that the crane has stood dead for a year and that they are carrying the salt aboard by hand before the storms.

6. Facundo lifts the heavy iron hook with both arms, but it slips straight out of the old chain ring. Fiona looks at the two parts and does not dare begin, because whatever she builds will not look right. Saira cannot decide between rope and wood, until Sarah jokes that a pirate is allowed to try both before supper — therefore Saira laughs and fetches both.

7. Fiona carves a wedge out of a barrel stave and drives it in beside the hook, so the hook cannot slip out of the ring again. The crane swings salt barrels aboard until dark and the whole quay cheers, but the work has eaten a full day of the good weather. With her own dockworkers cheering around her, Malva must give this crew the harbour; she says the chain comes down at first light and not one minute sooner.

8. Fiona hands the map to Facundo and asks him to lock it in the chart box, but fiddles start on the quay, so he sets it down on the deck and climbs back ashore. In the dusk Malva's two rowers come alongside the empty ship and lift the map off the planks. Sarah sees a boat pull away from the Sturmfeder, but she thinks it is a fisherman, therefore she says nothing.

9. At first light the dockworkers lower the chain, but Malva's berth is empty: the Eisenmöwe sailed in the night with the map, hours ahead of them. Facundo says out loud that it is his fault. Fiona is not angry with Facundo, she is angry with herself, and she says they should turn back, because she cannot draw a chart she knows will be wrong.

10. Lorena plants herself against the mast and refuses to move the ship one metre towards home. Sarah talks for a whole hour about every line Fiona ever showed her, so the three rocks, the black cove and the shelf of sand come back one by one. Fiona takes charcoal and draws them on a piece of sailcloth; the drawing is crooked and smudged and she is ashamed of it, but she pins it to the mast.

11. They sail by that sailcloth into cold fog, which burns their last lantern oil and costs them an hour of the falling tide. Saira wants to change the course twice, but Fiona says they follow this cloth and nothing else. Two dolphins run beside the bow until the three rocks rise out of the fog exactly where the charcoal put them.

12. Fiona anchors the Sturmfeder in deep water outside the shelf of sand her cloth marks. The Eisenmöwe already lies inside the cove above that shelf, dragging the bottom with a grapple chain, but the chain snaps and is gone in the water. Malva shouts across that this cove belongs to her harbour, therefore they should sail on; nobody on the Sturmfeder moves.

13. The falling tide drains the cove until the chest shows in clear, shoulder-deep water. Fiona says out loud that she cannot lift it alone and asks her crew for help. Facundo wades in and slings the spare sail under the chest while Lorena holds the line steady and Saira lashes on the two empty barrels Facundo never stowed, so the chest floats slowly up until it breaks the surface.

14. The same falling tide sets the heavy Eisenmöwe down on the sand, therefore Malva must stand at her rail and ask the crew she shut out for a tow. Fiona names her price: the stolen map, in her hand, now. Malva does not give in at the first asking, but the water keeps dropping under her hull, so she passes the map across.

15. The Sturmfeder pulls the Eisenmöwe off the sand. On the wet deck Fiona opens the chest in front of both crews: old gold coins and a small brass compass, which she puts in her pocket, because a compass still works when a chart is crooked. Malva says the harbour chain will stay down for this ship, then she rows home without her grapple chain, without the map and without one coin.

16. Fiona rolls the recovered map shut on the deck, the wind turns, and the five stand at the kitchen table in Zurich again with rain on the glass. She pins the crooked charcoal sailcloth on the wall above the table, not the beautiful map, and the little brass compass turns slowly on the wood beside it. Fiona is proud of that ugly chart exactly the way it is.

Challenges taken:
1. Getting past Krummhafen's chain without giving up the map.
2. The map stolen in the night; Fiona must draw the chart she fears.

items.planLine: close-up — Julian — Julian's face turned down, eyes wide and wet, toward the ball already lying still among the leaves below the step — the ball is lost below and Julian is in tears
items.arc:
1. On an autumn morning Levin and Julian sit on their Velos on the Lindenhof in Zürich, under the bare trees. Levin says he wants to find a real dragon before the first snow comes. Julian pushes his ball into his rucksack, because he wants to play later.
2. They ride over the Rathausbrücke out of the city and up the hill Rabenegg. Warm air comes out of a black hole in the warm rock. They lean their Velos at the cave mouth, and Levin picks a brown scale, small as his hand, out of the wet beech leaves.
3. A dragon crawls slowly out of the hole. Julian is afraid and hides behind Levin. The dragon says politely that a big scale is missing from his wing, therefore he cannot fly.
4. He says two old mountain ravens worked that scale loose while he slept and needed the whole night to drag it up to the Windchopf. Without it he is cold and slow on the ground, so he cannot climb after them, but a scale holds again as soon as it sits back in its bare place. Levin says they will call him Fenn, and he promises to bring the scale back.
5. Nia comes racing up the slope and barks. Max rides behind her and shouts that Nia pulled up this hill road all morning and would not stop. Kiaan gets off his Velo last and asks Fenn quietly what happens if the scale stays up there.
6. Fenn says his family flies south at the first snow, so the scale must be back before dark, or he sits in this cave alone all winter. Levin says out loud that they will climb the Windchopf today.
7. At the fork an old sign says Windchopf, and Kiaan reads it out. Max holds the little old scale under Nia's nose so she learns Fenn's smell. Three paths go up, but Nia turns onto the middle one, therefore the four stay together behind her.
8. High on the ridge one stone step is missing. Julian looks at the gap and will not go, because he is afraid. Kiaan says the light is already going.
9. Levin lifts Julian over the gap. But the rucksack tips, and the ball bounces away down into the leaves below the step. Julian cries, then he walks on.
10. On the summit the fog is cold and grey. Two big ravens sit on a nest of grey wool. Kiaan whispers that their feathers are old and dull, but the loud raven croaks that the scale belongs to them now.
11. Levin holds out the little old scale in trade. The loud raven says it is cold. Levin waits quietly, and at last the silent raven speaks: they are old, their nest is cold, winter is near, and the dragon's scale is warm.
12. Both ravens shove the big scale deep under the wool and turn their backs. The fog goes dark as the afternoon cools. The four start down with empty hands, and Levin has nothing left to trade. He feels beaten.
13. Halfway down Levin stops, because he remembers the warm air at the cave door. He shouts up through the fog that the rock there stays warm all winter, and that the cave stands empty as soon as Fenn flies south.
14. The loud raven drops out of the fog and lands on the path. It says the ravens will take the cave, but the boys must fetch the scale and carry it down themselves, because raven wings needed a whole night to drag it up. It says that if the cave is cold, the boys carry it back up before night.
15. The four climb back up in the last light. The silent raven pushes the big scale out of the wool. Max wraps it in his pullover, and they carry it between them.
16. At the missing step Levin's arms are full of the heavy scale. Julian is afraid, but he jumps the gap by himself. Below the step he picks his ball out of the leaves and holds it tight.
17. At the cave the two ravens feel the warm air and hop into the mouth. Fenn tells them the wind cannot reach them in there. Julian holds the scale up, and Levin presses it into the bare place on the wing until it sits.
18. Fenn takes all four boys on his back, loops once over the Altstadt and the lake, and sets them down beside their Velos. He flies south to his family. Julian says, "I jumped by myself," and he is proud all the way home.

Challenges taken:
1. A dragon who cannot fly and cannot climb after his scale
2. A gap in the stone steps that Julian will not cross
3. Two cold old ravens who will not give the scale back
4. Their price: fetch and carry the heavy scale down yourselves

items.arc:
1. On a grey autumn morning Levin and Julian stand with their Velos at the Limmat, under the two towers of the Grossmünster, and Levin says that nobody in his kindergarten believes him that dragons are real. Therefore he wants to find one today. Julian pushes his ball into his rucksack, because he never rides without it.
2. Max rides up with his dog Nia and shouts that Nia can smell anything in the whole world. Kiaan comes after him and says quietly that dragons live in caves, and caves are up in the hills above the lake. Therefore the four push their Velos over the Rathausbrücke and ride out into the yellow woods.
3. High on the hill Nia sniffs and pulls hard off the path. She stops in front of a black cave, and there Julian finds a shining scale in the wet leaves.
4. A young dragon crawls out of the cave. On his wing there is a bare grey spot. He says his name is Karu, but Julian is frightened and steps behind Max.
5. Karu says the found scale is only a small one from his tail. His big wing scale blew across the saddle in the storm, and from the cave mouth he watched a boy carry it into the hut on the next summit; therefore he cannot fly.
6. Karu says the first snow comes tonight, and then his family flies to the warm rocks without him. Levin says: "We climb up and ask the boy for the scale, because Karu must fly tonight." He puts the small tail scale in his pocket.
7. They lean their Velos on the rock beside the cave and start to climb. Where the path forks, Karu calls after them that the boy walked the left way. Levin says they all take that way together, because Julian is small.
8. Fallen rocks lie across the left path. Max rolls the big ones aside and Kiaan carries the small ones down the slope, but the work takes a long time, and the sky turns dark grey above them.
9. Below the hut a brook runs fast and loud. Wet stones stick out of the water, but Julian will not step on them, because he is afraid. Therefore he throws his ball into the brook, and it drifts into a slow shallow place near the bank.
10. There the four wade across, holding hands. But the water pulls the ball away downstream, and Julian cries, because the ball was his.
11. On the summit a boy sits on the bench of the alp hut with the scale on a string round his neck. Behind the window his mother packs boxes, because the hut shuts for the winter tomorrow. The boy says his name is Rico and that he found the scale himself.
12. Levin asks Rico for the scale for Karu. Rico says no, because in the storm he saw the dragon fly over the hut, and his whole class laughed at him; the scale is his only proof. Then he goes inside and shuts the door.
13. Max hammers on the door and Kiaan calls at the window, but Rico does not come out. The first snow falls on the roof.
14. The four go down with empty hands. At the cave Karu hears his family calling high above the clouds and answers them, but he cannot lift off; he lies down in the snow. Levin is ashamed, because he promised.
15. Then Levin remembers the morning at the river, when nobody believed him either. Therefore he says: "Rico does not want the scale. Rico wants somebody who believes him." They climb the mountain a second time through the snow.
16. Levin knocks and tells Rico that a real dragon lies in the cave, and that all four of them will stand up in his class and say it. Julian steps out from behind Max and holds the small tail scale out to Rico, for him to keep.
17. Rico takes the tail scale, then he comes down the mountain with them and lays the wing scale in Karu's claw. Karu presses it into the bare place, and it fits.
18. Karu calls up through the clouds to his family, then he lifts the four boys, Rico and Nia over the old town and the two towers by the river. Levin holds tight and cannot stop laughing.

Challenges taken:
1. Rock slide across the climb — costs time
2. Fast brook — costs Julian's ball
3. Rico refuses and shuts the door
4. Karu grounded in the snow, promise broken

items.arc:
1. On a hot summer morning Levin and Julian stand with their Velos on the Gemüsebrücke over the Limmat (real landmark: *Rathausbrücke (Zürich)*); Levin switches his new Velolampe on and off because he likes how bright it is, and he says he wants to find a real dragon cave today, because dragons are the best thing there is.
2. They ride out of the city and up a green hill; Julian pedals slowly in the heat, therefore Levin waits for his little brother at every bend.
3. High up they find a dark cave mouth, so Levin shines his lamp into the black opening; in the grass beside it a small scale shines faintly on its own, and he puts it in his trouser pocket.
4. A dragon walks out of the cave, and on one wing a jagged gap is bare; Levin is not afraid, because a dragon is exactly what he wished for.
5. Nia bursts out of the bushes, sniffs Levin's pocket and whines; Max pushes his Velo behind her and shouts that his dog has pulled him and Kiaan uphill all morning, and Kiaan says quietly that Nia smells everything that shines.
6. The dragon says that two grey guards of the Grauhorn tore the big scale off his wing while he slept and carried it up to their crack, and that the small flake in Levin's pocket broke off in the same night; without the big scale he cannot fly home over the Grauhorn, and he sounds tired.
7. Julian calls him Fauchi because his breath hisses, therefore the name stays, and Levin says out loud: "We will get the big scale back, or Fauchi never gets home."
8. Above the last pasture the path turns into narrow stone steps, so the four boys lay their Velos in the grass; Levin unclips his lamp and puts it in his pocket, because from here everything must be walked.
9. At a yellow signpost three paths split apart and Levin turns from one to the next without deciding, but Kiaan reads the middle arm aloud — "Grauhorn" — and Nia pulls that way, so they all take it; a fallen stone blocks the steps, therefore Max leans his shoulder against it while Nia digs at its foot until it rolls aside, and the pushing costs them so much time that the sun stands low.
10. From a rock high above, the two grey guards look down and call, "Go home. Nothing up here belongs to you"; Julian is afraid, but Levin takes his hand and keeps climbing.
11. On the summit the boys see where the guards live: a black crack in the rock with two stone beds inside, and the big wing scale lies at the front and shines so faintly that the beds stay in the dark.
12. Levin asks politely for the scale; the guards say their crack is cold and black, that they hoped the scale would light it and it never did, but that this weak shine is the only light they have, therefore they say no.
13. Julian holds his small flake up beside the big one — same shine, same pattern — so the guards stop arguing and admit the scale is Fauchi's, but the bigger guard shoves it deep into the crack and lies down across the opening.
14. The sun goes behind the ridge and the summit turns cold; Julian cries, and Levin believes his promise is broken, because the scale is now hidden under a guard.
15. Then Levin remembers what is in his pocket; he switches on his Velolampe, the whole black crack turns bright to the last stone bed, and he holds the lamp out and says the guards may keep it if they push the scale back into the grass.
16. The guards drag the scale out while Levin sets the burning lamp between their beds; he says he will miss his lamp, but all four boys and Nia carry the heavy scale down the steps to the cave.
17. They press the scale into the jagged gap on Fauchi's wing, where it locks fast, therefore Fauchi lifts off the ground and carries the four boys and Nia once over the old roofs of the Altstadt and the shining Limmat (real landmark: *Altstadt von Zürich*), and Levin laughs so loudly that Julian laughs too.
18. Fauchi sets them down beside their Velos, so Levin holds out the little flake to give it back, but Fauchi presses it into the empty lamp holder, where it glows; the four ride home side by side over the Gemüsebrücke, and Levin is proud, because his Velo now carries a light nobody else in Zurich has.

Challenges taken:
1. Steps stop the Velos — the bikes are left behind.
2. The fork and the fallen stone — time lost, sun sinking.
3. The guards refuse; the proof makes them bury the scale.
4. The low point turned by Levin giving up his lamp.

items.arc:
1. On a grey October afternoon Ayan and Liz walk along the wet quay at Ouchy, under the round tower of the Château d'Ouchy; Liz holds her doudou souris and says she is looking for a fairy, because fairies sleep in autumn leaves.

2. Maman walks behind them and says, "Stay in the middle, the stones are slippery"; Sarah keeps her big scarf folded over her arm, because she will not go near cold water.

3. Liz pushes the red leaves into a pile for the fairies and finds a piece of blue glass, which she keeps in her fist; Ayan stands at the boat museum window and says he will be the knight-captain of the old barque in the photograph, *La Nivéole*.

4. Maman turns to talk with Sarah, therefore nobody is watching when Liz leans over the edge for a second piece of blue glass; Liz slips on the wet leaves, and the doudou souris falls into the lake and sinks.

5. Liz screams and kicks the stones, and Maman kneels on the bottom step and reaches into the water, but her arm is too short and she cannot see the bottom; therefore Ayan says the mouse must come back before dark, because Liz sleeps with it and is afraid of the dark without it.

6. A pink fairy and a yellow fairy climb out of Liz's leaf pile; the pink one says, "You built our pile, so we come with you," but the yellow one says she is the only lamp down there and cold water eats her light.

7. A green fairy and a blue fairy come after them down the stone stairs, and the lake takes the children's legs and gives them silver tails, so they breathe under the water; Maman holds the top step and calls their names, and Sarah waits behind her with the scarf.

8. They swim down behind the yellow light onto the deck of *La Nivéole*, the barque from the photograph, where the doudou souris lies in the sand; under the keel an old crayfish backs away from the fairy light.

9. The crayfish creeps out toward the light, takes the mouse in both claws and pulls it into the cabin; he says his hole under the keel is black all winter, so he will trade the mouse for something bright.

10. Liz opens her hand, looks at the blue glass and shouts twice that it is hers because she found it; therefore the crayfish turns and carries the mouse toward the back of the cabin.

11. Ayan cannot wait, so he grabs for the mouse, but the crayfish slips into the black hold where the yellow light does not reach, and now the mouse is farther away than before.

12. The water above has gone grey with dusk and the yellow light is thin, so Ayan says that when it dies they must go up with nothing; he says out loud that he is afraid of the dark, and he asks the blue fairy to stay at his shoulder.

13. The green fairy sits on Liz's nose and counts four bubbles with her, in, out, in, out, therefore Liz stops shaking; Liz asks the yellow fairy to come into the hold with her, because she will not go into the black alone, and Ayan says, "A knight holds the door," and holds it against the current.

14. Inside the hold Liz sets the blue glass down in front of the crayfish, and the last of the yellow light catches in the glass, so the black hole turns blue; the crayfish gives back the doudou souris and keeps the glass, and Liz carries the mouse out past Ayan's arm.

15. They climb the stone stairs and the lake gives back their legs, and the four fairies go into the leaf pile as the first lamp on the quay lights; Sarah wraps the wet mouse in her scarf, and Liz says, "I went into the dark, and I came back."

Challenges taken:
1. Getting a sunken doudou out of the lake before the light dies.
2. Liz's temper and her refusal to give up her own treasure.
3. Going into the dark — Liz alone inside, Ayan at the door.

items.planLine: close-up — Kiaan — Kiaan crouches with one hand cupped toward the warm glow under the dark wet leaves, his face lit from below — a hidden light under the leaves has been found
items.arc:
1. At the Bahnhofplatz, Levin and Julian climb into the tram up to the Zürichberg, with two Guetzli in Levin's coat pocket; Julian holds his brother's sleeve the whole way, because he says he is much too small for such a long trip.
2. At the hedge along the fence of the Zoo Zürich two unknown boys are digging after a football; Max pulls his ball out, says his name and says his ball always rolls into the very worst place, but Kiaan says his name quietly and points at a light under the wet leaves.
3. Levin says his name and Julian's, then pushes the cold leaves aside: an egg as big as a school bag lies in the ground, warm and trembling, and it shines out over all four of them.
4. A green dragon comes over the beeches, screams once and drops straight at the children, but the thick branches stop her, therefore she climbs back and sits on a bare rock high above the forest, and Max says nobody could ever climb up there.
5. Julian is frightened, but he says the thing inside shall be called Funkli; Levin sees a wide flattened track running from the egg up the hill to that same rock, therefore he says Funkli rolled down from up there.
6. Levin says Funkli must get back under the rock before the shell opens, because a small dragon alone in the cold leaves is lost, and the open grass below the rock is the only ground where the mother can come down.
7. The egg is far too heavy to carry, therefore Kiaan says quietly that Funkli must not lie in the cold and pulls off his rain jacket, and the four roll Funkli onto it and drag it uphill.
8. Julian says he is too small to pull, therefore he walks beside the sledge and lays leaves over the shell; whenever the leaves slip and the light shines out, the mother drops at them, but the beech branches stop her every time, therefore she screams and climbs back to her rock.
9. Max goes in front and pulls the brambles out of the way, and the wet ground smears mud over the shell until no light shows at all, therefore the mother stops coming; Kiaan is cold without his jacket.
10. The path gets steep and the sledge jolts over a root, therefore a thin crack runs across the shell; Julian falls into the wet leaves, and he is cold and hungry.
11. Julian says they should leave Funkli here and go home for hot chocolate, but Levin says nobody leaves Funkli alone in the dark, therefore he gives Julian his last Guetzli and pulls the sledge on alone, and he stays hungry himself.
12. The slope tips sideways, therefore the egg slides off the jacket and rolls into a hollow under a fallen beech; Levin reaches in, but his shoulders are too wide, and Max does not fit through the small hole either.
13. Levin says Julian is exactly the right size; Julian is afraid of the dark hole, but he crawls in alone and shoves Funkli out into the light, where the others catch the egg on the slope.
14. The four drag Funkli onto the open grass below the rock, where the crack is wide now and Funkli knocks against the shell from inside.
15. The mother flies over the clearing, but the mud hides the light and she does not look down, therefore she turns away over the city and is gone; the clearing goes dark, and Levin does not know what to do any more.
16. Then Levin remembers that she came every single time the light showed, therefore he rubs the mud and the leaves off the shell with his sleeve until the whole clearing is bright, and he pulls the others back under the trees, because she drops at anyone who stands beside Funkli.
17. The mother lands on the grass next to the shining egg, the shell breaks open along the crack, and Funkli climbs out wet and squeaking; she carries him up to the rock, and from up there he squeaks down at the four children.
18. In the tram down the Zürichberg, Kiaan wears his muddy jacket again, and Julian sits at the window and says he was the only one small enough — and he feels big.

Challenges taken:
1. Moving an egg too heavy to carry
2. The mother dropping at them whenever the light shows
3. The egg lost in a hollow only the smallest fits into
4. The mother gone, the shell cracking, no light left to call her

items.planLine: close-up — Julian — Julian presses his cheek to the egg, eyes half-closed, a small smile on his face — the egg is warm like a stove tile and something may be alive inside
items.arc:
1. On a cold autumn afternoon Levin (5) walks with his little brother Julian (3) through the red and yellow leaves on the Lindenhof, and Levin, who loves dragons, says they are hunting dragon tracks.
2. Julian kneels between the roots of the big linden and digs out an egg as big as a football, therefore Levin knocks on it and the shell answers hard like a stone; Julian lays his cheek on it and says it is warm like a stove tile.
3. Kiaan (3), who is sitting on the other side of the trunk with his book, looks up and says an egg that goes cold never wakes.
4. Max (3) comes round the tree with his dog Nia and says he saw the egg first, therefore Julian hugs it and will not hand it to anybody.
5. The wind from the lake cools one side of the shell, but Levin says nothing because the two boys are strangers and his ears go hot; then he wants the little one to live more than he wants to stay quiet, therefore he says his name and asks theirs.
6. Levin says nobody owns the egg, but their mother keeps the tiled stove warm at home and they must get there before dark; Julian strokes the shell and calls the little one Ofeli.
7. Max wants to carry Ofeli himself, but Kiaan says Levin's stove is the nearest warm place, therefore all four go down the steep steps at Julian's pace, because Julian refuses to be carried and Levin leaves nobody behind.
8. Down by the river the wind is colder, therefore Levin pulls off his own jacket, knots it loosely round Ofeli in Julian's arms and walks on in his pullover.
9. On the Rathausbrücke Frau Brunner is packing her stall, an apple basket beside a crate of pumpkins, and she calls out that these are the last pumpkins of her year.
10. Julian slips on a wet leaf, therefore Ofeli rolls out of the loose jacket, over the bridge stones and into the pumpkin crate.
11. Frau Brunner says a woman paid her that morning for her biggest pumpkin, and Kiaan sees her stand the sold card against Ofeli in the crate.
12. Levin wants to tell her it is an egg but no word comes out, therefore Max shoves past the table to grab Ofeli and the apple basket goes over.
13. Frau Brunner pushes the crate onto her handcart, says she will not be fooled by four small boys and sends them away; it is dark now, Julian cries into Levin's pullover, and Levin sits down among the apples because nothing is left to try.
14. Then Levin remembers what Julian said under the linden, therefore he stands up and tells Frau Brunner the whole truth: it is an egg and not a pumpkin, Max knocked the apples over, their pockets are empty, and they will pick up every single one.
15. All four crawl over the bridge in the lamplight while the last shutter rattles down and Frau Brunner waits with her arms crossed, and Levin finds his jacket under the apples and puts it back on.
16. Levin asks her to take the pumpkin in her two palms, therefore she lifts it out of the crate; it is warm, and then it knocks against her hands from the inside, so she says she has sold pumpkins for thirty years and never a warm one, wraps it in her wool sack and gives it back, and says the woman will get her money again.
17. At the flat their mother opens the door and lets the four boys and Nia in, therefore Ofeli lies by the tiled stove, the shell cracks, and a small dragon climbs out and sneezes a spark that makes them all laugh.
18. The next morning they carry Ofeli back to the linden, because Levin wants him to see the tree he came from, and Ofeli lifts off Levin's hands for a crooked first flight and sets three-toed marks in the red leaves; Levin says those are the dragon tracks he was hunting, then he asks Max and Kiaan first whether they will come again tomorrow, and he feels proud.

Challenges taken:
1. Four strangers, one egg, one shy boy who must speak.
2. Getting the cooling egg down the hill at a three-year-old's pace.
3. The egg lost into a market crate that is already sold.
4. Winning it back with truth, work against a closing market, and warmth as proof.

items.planLine: close-up — Emma's face, alarmed — the bell rings and the crowd surges and her tricorn is knocked from her head — the tricorn is lost in the crowd
items.arc:
1. On a grey autumn morning Emma and Noah stand with Daniel on the misty, wet stones of the quay at the Hafen Enge in Zürich, in the pirate costumes Daniel sewed, pressed in among hundreds of onlookers; Noah says they must reach the front railing before ten, because at ten the bell rings, the lines come in, and the old sailing ship Nebelmöwe sails out for the last time and never again.

2. Emma sees only coats and legs and is impatient, therefore Daniel lifts her onto his shoulders; from up there she sees a woman in a blue coat at the ship's rail who calls down that she has only one deckhand left and needs two more hands at the sail, and Emma says she wants to be one of those hands.

3. The bell rings and the crowd pushes forward, so Emma's tricorn is knocked off her head and disappears under the shoes; Emma is frightened and cross.

4. Emma slides down and crawls between the legs of the grown-ups to look for her hat, but she finds instead a navy-blue captain's cap with a gold anchor, wet from the stones, so she puts it on and is delighted.

5. As she stands up, a boy in a homemade pirate coat is holding her tricorn; he says his name is Kilian, that he pulled the hat out from under the shoes, that he heard the woman call for hands, and that a real captain's cap will prove he belongs on that ship, therefore he demands the trade — but Emma holds the cap with both hands and refuses.

6. At the chestnut stand Hans, who has roasted Marroni beside this quay for years, gives Emma and Noah one hot chestnut each and says that the woman in the blue coat is Kapitänin Sarah, that he saw her lose that cap in the crush, and that she went aboard without knowing where it fell.

7. Emma's hands are full, so she puts her Marroni in her coat pocket and starts to push the cap under her coat, but she stops, because Noah says the owner is standing up there and that whoever carries the cap forward will be seen out of hundreds; Emma is torn, yet she leaves the cap on her head and decides to bring it back.

8. Daniel stays at the stand to pay and forgets to hold on, therefore the next surge shoves him backwards with the dry jackets and the chestnut bag, and he calls that the two should work their way to the rail and wait for him there; Emma is afraid without him.

9. The wall of grown-ups is too thick for Noah, but Emma is small enough to crawl underneath, so Noah tells her to crawl ahead and keep shouting his name; it is dark down there between the legs and Emma is frightened, but she goes.

10. Emma comes out at the front railing as the church clock strikes ten, and Kilian, small enough to use the gap she has opened, squeezes out beside her; Noah forces his way through behind them both.

11. The one deckhand has to haul in the gangway alone, therefore he leaves the last stern line lying loosely looped over the iron bollard and runs forward to the sail, and the Nebelmöwe begins to slide away from the stone edge.

12. Kilian waves the tricorn and shouts, but Kapitänin Sarah is watching the water and not the quay, and the shouting of two children is lost among hundreds of shouting people; Emma is close to tears.

13. Noah seizes the slack line as it slips towards the edge, but one boy alone cannot hold it, and Kilian says he takes orders from nobody's crew and runs to the empty place where the gangway stood; therefore Emma grips the line behind Noah, and together they drag one turn of it around the iron bollard and hold on.

14. The turn holds, so the Nebelmöwe stops a hand's breadth from the stone; Kapitänin Sarah looks over the rail, sees her line stretched down to the bollard and her cap with the gold anchor on the smallest pirate, and has the gangway run out again.

15. Emma climbs up and lays the cap in Sarah's hands herself and says it belongs to her, so Sarah puts it on and takes the two of them aboard as her hands at the sail; Daniel reaches the gangway with the dry jackets, and because Emma will not sail without him, Sarah calls him aboard too.

16. Emma asks for her hat, therefore she throws her hot Marroni down to Kilian, who stands alone beside the empty gangway place and throws the tricorn up to her; Emma wears it at the bow between Noah and Daniel while the black skull sail fills, and she says she is proud, because she gave the cap back with her own hands.

Challenges taken:
1. Reaching the front of a crowd too thick for them.
2. Keeping the found cap or giving it back, with a rival demanding it.
3. Holding the ship at the bollard after it has cast off.

items.arc:
1. On a cold autumn morning Levin brings his little brother Julian over the Bahnhofplatz to the Zürich Hauptbahnhof to watch the trains; the air smells of wet stone and hot Marroni, and Levin walks close to the wall, because he is shy and says hello to nobody he does not know; then Julian stops, because something shines in the red leaves.
2. It is an egg, big as a football and warm in the hands, and it glows like a lantern; Levin lifts it out of the leaves and says that no animal he knows lays an egg like this, but that a dragon does.
3. Julian knocks twice on the shell with one finger and the egg blinks twice; Levin knocks twice on the kerbstone beside it and the egg blinks twice again, so Levin says out loud, "It answers two knocks."
4. In the big hall under the station clock a dog runs at them with her nose down and pushes at the egg; Max comes after her and shouts that his dog Nia followed that warm smell all the way from the square and that he has been hunting this thing since morning; Levin holds the egg tight and says nothing at all.
5. Kiaan comes alone from the river side, out of breath, and says quietly that at dawn a big dragon came down on the wet steps of the Wasserkirche and has been sitting there since; Max says he himself saw something fall past the two towers of the Grossmünster and over the Bahnhofplatz; Levin believes them, because the two stories fit together.
6. Levin feels that the egg is cooler now than it was in the leaves; Kiaan says that in his dragon book an egg must stay warm or the young one never comes out, therefore it has to be back with the big dragon before the cold night; Julian is afraid.
7. Levin decides out loud, "Then we bring it to her, all four of us, before it is dark," and he gives the egg a name, Flämmli, because it glows; Max says the tram at the Bahnhofquai goes straight down along the river.
8. At the tram stop Levin trips over Nia's leash, because he is clumsy; Flämmli falls, rolls away between suitcases and legs and is gone, and the tram leaves without them.
9. All four crawl over the floor and search; Julian is the smallest, so he sees the glow under a bench and pulls it out; Levin is ashamed of his fall and gives Flämmli to Max to carry, although he has known Max for one hour.
10. Now they have to walk, so they go along the Limmat past the old guild houses to the Gemüsebrücke, where a market stands full of Räbeliechtli for the parade this evening.
11. Julian smells the Marroni and pulls Max's sleeve towards the stand; Flämmli slips out of Max's arm and rolls under a stall.
12. The lantern man picks it up, holds it over his head and calls it the finest lantern he has ever seen; he hangs it high on a hook, because this evening he walks at the front of the Räbeliechtli parade and wants the brightest light there.
13. Max asks loudly for it back, Kiaan asks politely twice, Levin cannot get one word out; they carry crates of turnips for the man, but he thanks them and keeps Flämmli, and while they work the sun goes down behind the trees of the Lindenhof.
14. The man lights all his lanterns and walks with Flämmli into the parade along the Limmatquai.
15. From the bridge the children see hundreds of lanterns and every single light looks the same; far below on the dark water the big dragon calls and does not come up; Julian cries, and Levin thinks that Flämmli is lost for good.
16. Then Levin remembers the kerbstone in the leaves and knocks twice on the stone railing of the bridge; far ahead in the row one single lantern blinks twice, and Nia barks at it.
17. They push through the crowd until they stand in front of the man, and Levin looks up at him and says loudly, "That is not a lantern, that is a baby dragon"; the man laughs and holds Flämmli higher, so Levin promises him the glowing shell for his hook, and the man walks down to the water with them, because such a light he will never find again.
18. On the wet steps of the Wasserkirche the shell splits open in the man's hands and Flämmli climbs out, and the big dragon comes down out of the dark and carries him up over the two towers; Levin is happy, and he asks Max and Kiaan whether they are coming again tomorrow.

Challenges taken:
1. Trusting two strangers who want the same egg
2. Flämmli lost on the station floor, the tram gone
3. The lantern man takes Flämmli and will not give him back
4. One light among hundreds in the parade

items.arc:
1. On a cold autumn afternoon Levin sits with his little brother Julian under the big lindens on the Lindenhof, high above the roofs of Zurich, where the towers of the Grossmünster stand up out of the city; Julian's hands are cold, therefore Levin warms them inside his jacket; Levin's red wool cap is on his head, Julian's ball lies in the leaves, and down the slope a heap of raked red and yellow leaves stands higher than a table.
2. Julian hears a soft hum under the roots, therefore he pushes the leaves apart between two thick roots and touches something round as a football and warm as a stove tile.
3. But two strange boys are kneeling at the other side of the same trunk with their hands on the same warm thing: Max says loudly that his hand was there first, because his dog Nia pulled him to these roots, and Kiaan says quietly that he came after the crow, which carries bright things into a hole in the fountain wall.
4. None of the four boys knows the others, therefore they say their names before anything else; Julian takes the warm thing in both arms and calls it Lindi, after the linden.
5. Levin says Lindi is a dragon egg, because his dragon book shows one just like it, and he says Lindi must still be warm when the dark falls, or it will never hatch; all four want to keep it warm.
6. Kiaan says a dragon egg needs a nest of leaves, because the crow's chicks sat in a nest of leaves and sticks up there in spring; all four believe him, so nobody thinks of hands or jackets, but Levin cannot decide where the nest should go.
7. Levin walks them to the Lindenhofbrunnen and back and says "or maybe over there" so often that the last warm sun slides off the fountain steps; Max stamps his feet and says they have to start now, therefore Levin is ashamed.
8. They line the root hollow with dry leaves, push Levin's wool cap under Lindi and hear the hum grow louder, so they know the nest works; Levin's ears are cold without the cap, but he talks and talks about his book, which shows a new dragon sneezing warm sparks at its first breath.
9. But the wind from the lake sweeps over the hill and strips the leaves out of the hollow, so the nest is gone; they gather leaves again, slower and colder than before, and Max calls Nia to lie along the open side as a wall against the wind.
10. Then the crow drops out of the branches and hacks at the warm shell, because it wants Lindi for its hole; Max shouts and Nia barks it off the egg, but the crow snatches the red wool cap out of the nest and stuffs it into the hole in the fountain wall.
11. Levin grabs Lindi to hold it safe, but he trips over a root, so Lindi rolls down the slope into the big heap of raked leaves.
12. They dig through the wet cold leaves for a long time and do not find Lindi, therefore Levin is afraid he has spoiled everything; but Julian throws his ball into the heap, it knocks against something hard, and one thin thread of steam rises above that spot.
13. They dig there and lift Lindi out; but the hum is slow now and the steam thins away, so Julian can hold the bare shell in both hands and feel no warmth at all, and he is frightened.
14. They carry Lindi back to the hollow and pile fresh leaves over it, but the cap is gone and the leaves stay cold; Kiaan holds his ear to the shell and says the hum has stopped.
15. The first lamps come on below the hill and the crow waits in the branches above them; Levin says it is his fault, because he took too long to choose, therefore Julian cries.
16. Then Levin remembers Julian's cold hands in his jacket that afternoon, so this time he does not think twice: he lifts Lindi out of the cold nest, holds it against his chest inside his jacket and tells Max, Kiaan and Julian to sit tight around him with their backs to the wind and Nia in front.
17. The crow dives once more, but it cannot reach through four backs and a dog; they sit still for a long time, until the shell cracks and a small dragon climbs out and sneezes warm sparks, so the crow flies off over the roofs with nothing.
18. Levin takes his cap back out of the empty hole in the fountain wall, therefore Lindi can sleep warm in a new leaf nest in the sheltered hollow behind the trunk; Lindi first breathes warm air on Julian's hands, so Julian laughs, and Levin laughs too, because he came up the Lindenhof with one brother and goes down it with three friends.

Challenges taken:
1. Four strangers, one egg — agree or lose the time
2. Keep a leaf nest warm against the lake wind
3. The crow: cap stolen, egg lost in the leaf heap
4. The shell goes cold before dark

items.planLine: close-up — Julian — Julian trips over a thick root and lands on his hands beside a hollow in the earth — the hollow under the root is found
items.arc:
1. Autumn afternoon on the Lindenhof: Levin, who is five, kicks red and yellow leaves with his brother Julian, who is three. Levin says he is looking for dragon tracks, because dragons are what he likes best. Their mother gave Levin a warm paper bag of Marroni and said they must be home before dark. Julian trips over a thick linden root.

2. In the hollow under the root lies an egg, as big as a football and warm like a stove tile. Levin puts his ear against it, therefore he hears it knock once from inside. Levin is amazed.

3. A ball rolls against Levin's shoe, and two boys come after it. Max talks fast: "Ich bin Max. Ich habe das Ei zuerst gesehen!" Kiaan says it quietly: "Ich heisse Kiaan. Es zittert."

4. All four hold the egg at the same moment, and nobody lets go. The shell cools in their cold hands, therefore the knocking stops. Levin wants to say his name, but he is too shy, so Julian says it for him: "Das ist Levin. Ich bin Julian."

5. About the egg Levin does speak, and loudly: "Warm heisst wach. Kalt heisst schlafen. Bis es dunkel ist, muss es warm bleiben." He pushes the egg into his jacket against the hot Marroni bag, therefore the knocking comes back, and Kiaan counts three knocks. Julian calls it Flämmli, and all four carry it together, because nobody owns it.

6. Julian points up and is frightened, because a big shadow slides over the roofs and circles low above their linden. Levin shows the others three small three-toed prints in the earth beside the root. Therefore he says a big dragon has been at this tree and is searching for its egg here.

7. The sun slips off the Lindenhof wall, the wind comes cold from the lake, and the shell goes cool even against the bag. Levin decides they must get out of the wind, therefore they leave the tree. Max says the last sun still lies on the Rathausbrücke over the water, so all four carry the egg down through the lanes.

8. In a narrow lane Julian is hungry. He takes the bag out of Levin's jacket and eats three Marroni, therefore the bag gets flat and cool. Kiaan counts the knocks, and they come slower, and Levin is worried.

9. Levin opens his jacket to look at the egg. A bigger boy on a Trottinett, Ramon, is picking stones out of an old wall; he sees the egg and says it is a fossil for his collection and that small boys have no business with it. Levin says nothing, but Kiaan says "Nein". Ramon rolls along beside them anyway.

10. On the Rathausbrücke the last sun lies on the stone, and the two towers of the Grossmünster stand over the water. Levin holds the egg in the sun, therefore it knocks four times, and Kiaan counts them. Levin tells Julian to stay away from the railing, because the Limmat runs below.

11. Ramon grabs at the egg, therefore Levin twists away. The bag falls out of Julian's hand. Max is fast and grabs after it, but the hot Marroni roll through the railing into the Limmat.

12. Ramon pulls the egg out of Levin's arms and finds it cold and dead quiet. He says: "Das ist ja nur ein Stein." His hands are cold and he needs both of them for his Trottinett, therefore he sets the egg on the bridge wall and rolls to the foot of the stairs.

13. The egg lies cold on the stone, the sun is gone behind the roofs, and the lanterns come on. Every Marroni is in the river, so there is nothing warm left. Julian cries, and Levin is sure that Flämmli will never wake.

14. Then Levin remembers that the big dragon circled their own linden, and that the egg stayed warm all afternoon against his body. Home is far, but the linden is straight up the stairs. Therefore he pulls off his jacket and wraps the egg in it, and he is cold at once.

15. All four press the bundle between them like four small ovens. Kiaan takes Julian's hand, because the steps are dark and Julian trips easily. They climb slowly, at Julian's pace.

16. At the foot of the stairs Ramon steps in front of them, the Trottinett under his arm, and wants his stone back. Levin, who could not even say his own name at midday, says loudly: "Es gehört dir nicht, und uns auch nicht." Max and Kiaan close in around the bundle.

17. The jacket bundle moves in Levin's arms, and Ramon sees it move. He wanted a stone and not an animal, therefore he steps aside and follows them up. At the roots the boys lay the jacket down, and the shell cracks.

18. Flämmli climbs out, licks Julian's hand and cries. On that cry the big dragon comes down onto the linden and lifts Flämmli away over the roofs of the Altstadt, while Ramon watches with empty hands. Levin has no jacket, no Marroni and no dragon, and he is happy, and he asks Max and Kiaan to come back to this tree tomorrow.

Challenges taken:
1. Four strangers hold one cooling egg and nobody lets go.
2. The wind rises and the warm bag runs out.
3. Ramon on the bridge: the Marroni are lost and the egg is abandoned cold.
4. Getting the cold egg up the hill with only their own bodies, past Ramon.

items.arc:
1. It is autumn on the Lindenhof, the wind comes cold from the lake, and Levin wears his red mittens while he shows his little brother Julian where dragon tracks would be if dragons walked in leaves, high above the towers of the Grossmünster.
2. At the foot of the old stone wall, between the roots of the big linden, they scrape the loose leaves aside and find an egg in a hollow of crumbly earth, as big as a football and as warm as an oven tile.
3. A football rolls round the trunk, therefore Max comes running after it, and from the other side of the roots he sees the same egg at the same moment and shouts that this is no ball because it steams.
4. Kiaan climbs down from the wall where he has been sitting, says his own name quietly first, and asks the other three what they are called, because none of them know each other.
5. Levin lifts the egg and says out loud what has to happen: an egg like this must stay warm, therefore it must be warm again before dark, or the little one inside will never come out.
6. The egg is cooling in the wind, but Levin cannot decide where to put it, therefore Max decides for him and points at the fountain rim, where the last sun still lies on the stone.
7. Tobias comes across the square with hands red from the cold, picks the egg up off the rim and says it is his ball now; Kiaan tells him that taking it is not fair, but Tobias only laughs.
8. Levin sees the cold red hands, therefore he pulls off his own red mittens and holds them out, and Tobias takes the mittens and puts the egg back into Julian's arms.
9. Julian carries the egg in both arms back to the linden, but on the way it grows cold, and at the roots he feels warm air on his hands, coming out of a gap in the old wall right above the hollow.
10. A big stone is wedged in that gap, therefore all four push it together, but it does not move a finger's width.
11. Levin wraps the cold egg in his scarf and holds it tight against him, therefore the shell grows warm again, and it cracks.
12. A small dragon climbs out, very warm and very quick; Julian names him Zünsli, and Zünsli creeps straight into the warm scarf and leaves a black smudge of soot on it.
13. Zünsli scratches at the wedged stone and peeps, and deep in the hill something peeps back, much lower and much bigger, and pushes at the stone from inside — but the stone sits fast.
14. Tobias comes back with a tin box under his arm, says he kicked that stone into the gap in the morning so nobody would find his hiding place, and sits down on the stone and shouts at them to go away.
15. It is dark now and the cold falls on the Lindenhof; Julian takes Zünsli out of the scarf into his hands, but Zünsli stops peeping and lies still, therefore Levin is afraid they have come too late.
16. Then Levin remembers the loose, crumbly earth of the hollow under the stone, therefore he grabs a fallen branch and digs with it and with his bare cold hands, Max and Kiaan dig beside him, and Tobias kicks earth back into the hole but cannot fill it as fast as three boys empty it.
17. The earth gives way under the stone, the stone tips over, and Tobias lands in the leaves; he sees a big eye blink in the open gap, therefore he grabs his box and runs home.
18. Zünsli crawls into the warm dark and peeps once more from inside, the four boys sit close together in the cold leaves, and Levin's hands are bare and cold, but the rest of him is warm through, because this time he decided himself and because he is not alone on the hill.

Challenges taken:
1. The cooling egg and Levin's indecision about where to warm it
2. Tobias takes the egg for a ball; buying it back costs Levin his mittens
3. The warm gap is blocked by a wedged stone that will not push
4. Tobias sits on the stone in the dark while Zünsli goes cold

items.arc:
1. On an autumn afternoon Levin, five, and his little brother Julian, three, kick through the red and yellow leaves on the Lindenhof; Levin wears his red wool cap and draws a dragon in the gravel, because he knows every dragon in his books at home and wants to see a real one.
2. Julian trips over a root of the big linden; between the roots lies an egg as big as a football, and it is warm like an oven tile.
3. On the other side of the same tree stand two boys they do not know: Max holds his dog Nia on the leash and says Nia smelled the warm thing first, and Kiaan kneels down close and says this is no stone.
4. Levin knows what a dragon egg needs, but he is too shy to talk to strangers, therefore he whispers to Julian that the egg must stay warm or the dragon inside will never wake, and Julian says it out loud for him.
5. Kiaan says nobody knows whose egg it is, therefore all four of them will carry it together; Julian agrees at once, and Levin nods.
6. Max says the old bakery house down in the narrow lane is warm, because Nia pulled him to the bread smell there this morning; Levin says yes at once, because his own home is far up the windy hill and the egg is already cooler.
7. Levin pulls off his jacket, keeps his cap on his head, and lays dry leaves inside the jacket; the four of them lift the egg in it, and it pulls heavy on their arms.
8. They carry it past the fountain, where the wind is sharp; the raven of their linden drops down and snatches a beakful of the dry leaves, and Levin sees wool already lying in its nest up in the branches.
9. The wind takes the rest of the leaves out of the open jacket, therefore the egg lies bare and cools fast; Julian calls it Fünkli and says Fünkli must not get cold.
10. Max points to the steep old stairs down into the lanes, but the steps are wet with leaves, Julian slips on the first one and his scarf slides away into the dark, and Levin says out loud that they would break Fünkli if they fell, therefore he takes them all the long flat way.
11. On the long way the raven flies ahead of them over the roofs; Kiaan says the hill gets cold the moment the sun leaves it, and the last sun goes off the roofs while they walk faster.
12. In the narrow lane the baker is pulling down her shutter; Levin wants to ask her for a warm corner, but no word comes out of him, and she locks the shutter and is gone round the corner.
13. Kiaan bends down and finds warm bread air breathing out of a low cellar window at street level, but the raven stands in the window well and picks up the dry leaves that have drifted in, and it does not move for Max's shouting, because those are the driest leaves in the whole lane.
14. Fünkli's shell is grey and hard now, Julian breathes on it and cries, and Levin sits down on the cold stones and says it is his fault, because he did not speak while the baker was still there.
15. Then Levin remembers the wool in the raven's nest; he pulls off his red cap, lays it three steps from the window and says loudly that the raven may keep it.
16. The raven hops to the cap, takes it in its beak and flies off over the roofs; Levin lifts Fünkli into the warm air of the cellar window, and the shell grows warm again under his hands.
17. The shell cracks and a small dragon climbs out onto Julian's knees and sneezes; Julian's neck is bare since the stairs, therefore he holds Fünkli against it and laughs, and Levin wraps his jacket round them both.
18. Back up on the Lindenhof the raven sits alone in the cold wind with the red cap in its nest and looks down at Fünkli in the warm jacket; Levin's head is cold and his arms are warm, and he says out loud to Max and Kiaan that all four of them will come again tomorrow.

Challenges taken:
1. Strangers over one egg — agreeing to carry it together
2. Carrying the egg warm; the raven takes the bedding
3. The wet stairs refused; the long way costs the last sun
4. The bakery is shut and Levin cannot speak
5. The raven blocks the one warm window
