items.arc:
1. On an autumn afternoon Levin, who is five and loves dragons, digs in the red and yellow leaves on the Lindenhof for treasure, while his little brother Julian, who is three, holds his hand, because the bigger boys on their Trottinetts ride loudly down the lane and up again past the wall; cold wind comes off the lake, and the grown-ups at the chess boards pack up and go.
2. Between the roots of the big linden lies an egg as big as a football and warm as an oven tile; Julian does not dare touch it, therefore Levin lifts it against his coat, and something inside knocks once.
3. Max comes round the trunk bouncing his football and says fast and loud that he saw it first and that it is his.
4. Kiaan comes round the other side of the same tree, lays both hands on the shell without a word, and then says quietly that he has read about eggs like this: an egg that gets cold falls asleep and never hatches.
5. All four hold the egg at once and tell each other their names; Julian whispers a name into his brother's ear, Levin says it out loud — Zippi — and Levin says that Zippi belongs to nobody and that they will keep him warm together.
6. The hollow between the roots is warm, because the sun has lain on that earth all day, therefore Levin lays Zippi carefully back into it, and the four kneel round it out of the wind.
7. Silvan, the biggest of the Trottinett boys, rolls up to see what four small boys are kneeling around; he lifts Zippi out of the hollow, says that he has it now and so it is his and that the boys at the wall have never seen a find that knocks, and he rides off down the lane — Levin shouts for a grown-up, but the square is empty in the cold.
8. A Trottinett cannot ride steps, so Levin takes Julian's hand and runs down the steep steps to the Schipfe, telling him to hold the railing, while Silvan has to go the long way round through the lane.
9. Down by the Rathausbrücke Silvan's front wheel sticks in wet leaves and mud and he wobbles with the egg under one arm; Levin sees that he will fall on top of Zippi, therefore he calls the others to hold Silvan up, and Max drops his football in the mud to take Silvan's arm with both hands.
10. Silvan pulls his boot free, but then he cannot keep hold of the egg; it falls, and Julian catches it against his jacket the way he catches a ball, and Zippi knocks twice against him.
11. Julian pushes the egg straight into Levin's arms, because he is sure he will drop it, and Max's football stays behind in the mud of the dark lane; Levin carries Zippi up the hill under his coat, and it knocks the whole way.
12. Silvan pushes his Trottinett up the lane behind them, because the boys at the wall are up there and the knocking thing is still not his.
13. On the Lindenhof the sun is long gone; the four set Zippi back into the hollow between the roots, but the earth is cold now, and the knocking stops.
14. Silvan reaches into the hollow, and Julian shouts "Nein!" out loud for the first time all day, but Silvan takes the egg anyway, turns it over, says it is only a cold stone, drops it in the leaves and goes to the wall empty-handed.
15. Levin sits down in the dark and says they came too late; Julian cries, because he believes Zippi will never wake up.
16. Then Levin says what he saw himself: Zippi knocked against Julian's jacket at the bridge and under his own coat all the way up the hill, and both times it stopped on the bare ground, because the sun that warmed the hollow is gone — therefore they are the warm place now, and they will hold Zippi in turns inside their jackets, and Max will count.
17. Max counts every turn out loud, but after Max and Kiaan and Levin their arms are tired and the egg is still silent; Silvan comes over from the wall and says that if the thing wakes it is his, Levin says no, and Silvan stays and waits — and now it is Julian's turn, and Julian is afraid.
18. Julian sits down between the roots out of the wind and holds Zippi under his jacket with both arms until the shell cracks and the little dragon climbs out into his arms; Silvan holds out his hands, but Zippi presses into Julian's jacket and will not go to him, therefore Silvan takes his Trottinett and rides home with nothing, and Julian, in the lantern light, says the name out loud himself, so that everyone on the Lindenhof can hear it.

Challenges taken:
1. Four strangers claim one egg and must agree.
2. Silvan takes the egg and rides off downhill.
3. The stuck wheel: the egg must come back without falling.
4. The hollow is cold now; Silvan grabs again and drops a "stone".
5. Zippi is silent and the boys' arms give out before Julian's turn.

items.arc:
1. On a cold autumn afternoon Levin, five, and his little brother Julian, three, get a bag of hot Marroni from their mother at the chestnut stand on the Bahnhofstrasse, and she lets them play up on the Lindenhof if they stay by the big linden; Julian holds the steaming bag against his cheek, therefore Levin says that steam always means something is warm.
2. Between the roots of the biggest linden Levin sees steam rising out of the leaves, but two boys he does not know are digging into the same pile from the other side of the trunk, therefore all four lift the thing out together: an egg as big as a football, warm as a stove tile.
3. The loud boy says he is Max and that his dog Nia smelled it first, and Nia scrapes a scale as big as a plate out of the leaves; the quiet boy says he is Kiaan, keeps the scale in both hands and says the roots are hollowed out like a bowl; Levin is too shy to say his own name, therefore Julian says it for him.
4. A wide shadow slides over the leaves and a deep call comes from above the roofs, therefore the four boys duck; then a young dragon the size of a handcart glides down out of the linden branches onto the low wall, with wet leaf litter stuck to his claws.
5. He says his name is Turi, the egg is his little brother, and he has dug under every tree on this hill since this morning, therefore the boys must step back at once; Julian sits down in front of the egg and does not move.
6. Turi puffs at the shell to warm it, but only grey smoke comes out, and under Levin's hand the shell turns cool; Levin loves dragons and knows from his books that a cold egg never wakes, therefore he says out loud that the egg must be warm again before dark.
7. Julian is hungry, but he lays his bag of hot Marroni against the shell anyway and calls the one inside Flämmli.
8. The wind off the lake pulls the warmth straight off the bag, therefore the boys bank leaves over the egg and Max holds his jacket up against the wind, but the steam off the shell only gets thinner.
9. Levin feels that Turi's side is warm as a stove tile although his fire makes nothing but smoke, therefore he asks Turi to lie around the egg; Turi says no, because he means to put his brother back in these roots and hand him to his mother himself.
10. Max says the far side of the hill lies out of the wind, therefore the four boys lift the egg in Kiaan's jacket, two on each side — but Turi drops off the wall and pulls the bundle out of their hands.
11. The deep call comes again over the roofs, therefore Turi flinches; the smooth jacket slides out of his claws, and the egg rolls down the slope into the deep leaves along the wall.
12. The boys pull pile after pile apart under the lamps, but in the dark every pile looks the same, and Nia sniffs the whole wet wall without finding anything; Julian cries, and Max says the egg is gone for good.
13. Turi sits down in the leaves and says that his fire has never once lit, not a single time in his life, therefore the boys see that the one they were afraid of is the one who is frightened.
14. Levin remembers the steam he saw in the very first pile, therefore he tells everyone to kneel down and look flat along the ground, and he sends Turi to the piles by the wall while he takes the piles by the tree.
15. Levin finds one thin thread of steam at the wall, thinner than the first one; Nia digs, Kiaan pushes the big scale under the egg, and the four boys lift it out of the wet leaves, cool and quiet.
16. Levin lays the egg back into the root hollow, packs dry leaves around it and spreads three jackets over the top, then he tells Turi that he cannot make fire but he can be the warm wall; therefore Turi curls right around the nest, and the boys lie against his warm side out of the wind.
17. The shell knocks, then it cracks, and Flämmli climbs out as big as a cat and sneezes one small warm spark onto Julian's sleeve.
18. Turi lifts Flämmli onto his back and flies off over the roofs towards his mother's call, because he wants to tell her the truth himself; under the linden Levin says his own name out loud to Max and Kiaan and asks whether they want to come back to the hill tomorrow, and he is not shy any more.

Challenges taken:
1. A creature is on the path for reasons of its own — Turi guards the egg
2. Cold and no shelter (inverted heat/shade) — the wind strips every warmth away
3. Every leaf pile looks the same in the dark
4. Keep the found egg or hand it back

items.planLine: close-up — Julian — Julian clutches the warm paper bag of Marroni inside his jacket, chin down, arms crossed over it — the Marroni bag is introduced as Julian's guarded treasure
items.arc:
1. On a cold autumn afternoon Levin and his little brother Julian climb the long stairs up to the Lindenhof, where the leaves are red and yellow, the towers of the Grossmünster stand over the roofs, and the streets far below already lie in shadow.
2. Julian carries a warm paper bag of Marroni from a stand down in the street; he keeps it inside his jacket and will not give one away, not even to Levin.
3. Max comes up with his football and his dog Nia, Kiaan comes right behind him and says the wind from the lake bites, and the four play ball in the leaves.
4. The ball rolls into the roots of the big linden; Julian runs after it and finds an egg, as big as a football and as warm as an oven tile, wedged in the gap between two roots.
5. The gap is too narrow for their hands, so Levin pushes his Unihockey stick in and levers very slowly; the egg comes free, but the blade cracks.
6. Something knocks inside the shell, and Levin, who loves dragons, says a dragon baby is in there, that the colder it gets the quieter the knocking gets, and that then it may never come out.
7. Levin takes off his own jacket, wraps the egg in it and holds it against Julian's chest; Max asks for one Marroni for his cold hands, and Julian says no.
8. A young dragon walks up the hill out of the mist, says her name is Nebla, hears the four names and says the knocking called her, because this egg is from her family's nest.
9. Nebla lifts the egg out of Julian's arms and does not listen to Levin; Julian is frightened and hides behind his brother, and she carries the egg down the Lindenhof stairs into the mist.
10. Her warm breath hangs as smoke between the houses; Levin sees it and points, Max runs first with Nia at his heels, and the smoke leads all of them down to the Rathausbrücke, which everybody calls the Gemüsebrücke.
11. Nebla has set the egg into the cold stone corner of the bridge railing and says she will guard it there until dark and then walk it home; when Levin says the stone is cold, she plants herself in front of it and does not move.
12. Kiaan asks quietly whether he may listen; Nebla lets him, and Kiaan puts his ear to the shell and says the knocking has stopped.
13. Levin tries to lift the egg out of the stone with his stick, but the cracked blade bends and slips, so Nebla has to lift it herself; the bridge lamps come on, the egg lies still in her claws, and her waiting has come to nothing.
14. Levin says the way home is too long and too cold for the egg and that the leaf heap under the linden is the warmest place he knows, so they carry it back up the stairs, bury it in the leaves and cover it with all four jackets; the egg stays cold and still, and Julian cries.
15. Levin asks Nebla to curl around the egg and breathe her warm smoke on it; she turns away and says her flame is far too small, and when he asks a second time she says she dropped this egg this morning when she tried to fly, that she cannot fly yet, and that she is afraid to touch it again.
16. Julian, who has been frightened of her all afternoon, takes the warm bag of Marroni from inside his jacket, puts it in her claw and asks her to warm the little one; Nebla curls around the egg in the leaves and breathes.
17. The shell knocks again, then opens, and a small dragon climbs out onto Julian's knees; Julian says he is warm, and Max says then his name is Kachel.
18. Kachel is too small for the cold night, so Nebla carries him in her claws up the dark hill into the trees and says they will come back to the linden tomorrow; the lamps shine over the Lindenhof, and Julian waves with cold hands and says he is not afraid of dragons any more.

Challenges taken:
1. Egg wedged in a root gap too narrow for hands
2. A creature holds the egg and means to keep it
3. Following warm breath through mist when the taker is out of sight
4. The frightened one must be reassured before she will help

items.planLine: close-up — Levin — Levin holds the egg and looks at the low sun hanging behind the rooftops, his face worried — the danger to the egg is spoken aloud
items.arc:
1. On a cold autumn afternoon, Levin, his little brother Julian and their friends Max and Kiaan play ball on the Lindenhof, while Mama reads on a bench far across the square and high in the big linden, hidden among red and yellow leaves, a dragon sits by her empty nest.
2. The ball rolls between the roots of the big linden by the steps, so Julian crawls after it and finds an egg as big as a football and as warm as a stove tile.
3. Nobody knows whose egg it is, but Levin knows from his dragon books that a baby dragon can only hatch if its egg stays warm, and the sun already hangs low while the wind from the lake blows cold.
4. So Levin wraps the egg in his own jacket to carry it to Mama, even though now he is cold himself.
5. But the big dragon, red and yellow like the leaves, drops out of the linden crown, lands between the children and Mama's bench, and hisses.
6. Julian screams and hides behind Levin, so Levin grabs his hand, and all four run to the big chess figures.
7. Kiaan whispers that they must stand as still as chess figures, and they freeze while the dragon looks right past them and past the jacket.
8. Because she cannot find them, the dragon flies back up into the linden and calls "Huuum," and against Julian's ear the egg hums back, so softly that only he hears it.
9. Julian whispers that the dragon is the egg's mama, so the four walk toward the linden to give it back.
10. But Max runs two steps closer, waves both arms and shouts loudly, "Here is your egg!", and the dragon flinches and flaps up into the crown, and the wind of her wings makes Levin stumble.
11. The egg tumbles out of the jacket and rolls toward the steps, and Levin cries "Watch the steps!" as Max runs fast and catches it on the top step.
12. Now the dragon hides high in the crown and will not come down, and the sun sinks behind the roofs.
13. Levin will not lay the egg on the cold ground, where it would cool even faster, but he remembers how the dragon flinched when Max rushed and waved: she is afraid of loud children.
14. So Levin says the smallest and quietest must go alone, and Julian, who was so afraid, takes the egg in the jacket and walks slowly to the linden, while Levin waits at the chess figures with Max and Kiaan.
15. Julian sits down among the roots, holds the egg up where the dragon can see it, and stays as still and quiet as he can.
16. Then the dragon calls "Huuum" from the crown, the egg hums back against Julian's hands, and because only one small quiet boy sits below her and not four loud ones, she climbs down, says softly, "I am Rubina, the wind blew my egg out of my nest," and takes it gently in her claws.
17. Rubina breathes a small warm flame over the egg, and it glows and cracks, and a baby dragon blinks at the towers of the Grossmünster above the roofs.
18. Rubina nudges Julian thankfully with her nose, and the four friends stand close together while Julian feels proud, because he was afraid and went anyway.

Challenges taken:
1. Standing still like chess figures while the dragon looks past.
2. The egg rolls toward the steps and must be caught then.
3. The dragon's fright must be understood without words.
4. A frightened creature that will not come down must be coaxed.
5. The loud, big ones must hand the task to the smallest.

items.planLine: close-up — Fiona — Kapitän Zollingers Seekarte slides halfway out from behind the crooked frame as Fiona's fingers catch its edge — the chart is found
items.arc:
1. On a grey autumn afternoon at three, chestnuts fall on the cobbles in front of the Nationalmuseum as Fiona, Sarah, Saira, Facundo and Lorena go in wearing the pirate costumes they sewed together out of thin cotton, and Fiona, who sews every seam a second time, wears the wide sash she doubled out of sailcloth and carries her sewing scissors for any loose thread.
2. Because she cannot walk past a crooked old frame in a dusty corner, Fiona straightens it, and a real sea chart slides out from behind it: Kapitän Zollinger's chart, with a red cross on one stone in the old wall under the Lindenhof, above the Limmat.
3. But the guard, Herr Brunner, has seen the chart and strides toward them to lock it in the archive, where nothing found in his museum ever comes out again, so Fiona, who wants to dig out the captain's chest with her own hands, runs with it.
4. So Sarah steps into the narrow passage behind them and chatters questions at Herr Brunner about every suit of armour, and because he will not push a visitor aside, the others reach the back door to the river bank, and then Sarah slips past him and runs after her friends.
5. There, because the chart has left its hiding place, a pirate ship glides out of the fog on the Limmat, and her old steersman calls across that they are Kapitän Zollinger's crew, come for his chart; when Fiona gives her name and the names of her friends, he names the ship the Seeschwalbe and the parrot Pfeffer, who flies line ends through the rigging.
6. Facundo pulls Sarah over the rail one step ahead of Herr Brunner's hand, and the crew, who want their captain's chest raised at last and follow whoever holds his chart, warn that the Seeschwalbe comes only once and sinks back into the fog for good at sunset, so Fiona orders them up the river to the Lindenhof before the sun goes down.
7. But at the low bridge by the Hauptbahnhof the mast must come down, every rope aboard has gone brittle in two hundred years of fog, and when Facundo asks for Fiona's doubled sailcloth sash, the only cloth aboard that will not tear like their thin costumes, she refuses, because she will not spoil her perfect seams.
8. So the rope snaps, and Facundo shouts at everyone to duck and catches the falling mast on his shoulders so nobody is hit, but its tip strikes the bridge, and the yard from which Zollinger once reached his stone breaks off and drifts away.
9. Now the crew must row against the current, and although Saira grabs an oar and calls a fast stroke that brings them to the wall before sunset, Herr Brunner walks the short way through the old town and is on the Lindenhof long before them.
10. The crew hold the Seeschwalbe at the landing with their oars, right under the marked stone, but without the yard the deck lies far below it, the wall is smooth, the sun is sinking behind the hills west of the city, and Herr Brunner, looking down from the Lindenhof, runs for the steps to the landing, where whoever holds the chart can order the crew to pull away.
11. Then Fiona sees an old iron ring above the stone, whose mortar crumbled away long ago, and she cuts her own coat into strips with her sewing scissors and knots them into a rope, because she knows her doubled seams will hold her.
12. She gives the chart to Lorena, whom she trusts most, Pfeffer flies the rope's end through the ring and back down, and Facundo hauls Fiona up the wall, telling her to hold tight above the cold water.
13. Herr Brunner steps aboard and demands the chart, and Lorena wavers for a moment, but then she holds it behind her back and says no, and the crew, who obey whoever holds it, stand between her and him.
14. So Fiona, high on the wall, works the loose stone out with her scissors and her hands, lifts the small chest out of the earth behind it and ties it to her coat-rope, and Facundo lowers first the chest and then Fiona to the deck, the doubled seams holding where the old rope snapped.
15. As the sun goes down, the crew set the five friends, the chest and Herr Brunner ashore on the landing, the Seeschwalbe fades into the fog, and the friends open the chest on a heap of old silver coins; Fiona hands Herr Brunner the chart, which belongs to his museum, and while he stares at the open chest he was too slow to stop, Fiona stands in half a coat and laughs, prouder of it than of any perfect seam.

Challenges taken:
1. The smooth wall with nothing to grip above the deck.
2. A rope built from a sewn coat.
3. Rowing upstream against the current after the mast falls.
4. The chest lowered from a height without breaking.
5. Lorena refuses the chart to someone who keeps demanding it.

items.planLine: close-up — Sura — Sura's great grey head leans out of the mist, eyes heavy, as her deep tired voice answers the call — Sura has spoken: she will rise into the clouds alone with the big evening wind
items.arc:
1. On a foggy autumn afternoon, Levin, his little brother Julian and their friends Max and Kiaan play ball between the Wasserkirche and the Grossmünster.
2. The ball rolls to the old stone wall of the Grossmünster, and when Julian fetches it, he finds a scale as big as Levin's hand hanging on the stone, still warm, as if it had come loose only a moment ago.
3. Kiaan lifts the scale off, and behind it a path opens in the wall, leading into a world of mist and rocky peaks.
4. Levin wants to call "Hello?" into the mist, but he is shy and his voice is only a whisper, so Max calls loudly into the silence instead.
5. A deep, tired voice answers: "I am Sura, and I am old. Go home, children. When the big evening wind comes, I will rise into the clouds, alone and forever."
6. Levin loves dragons and does not want Sura to vanish alone, so the four step onto the misty path.
7. But the fog is so thick that Julian stumbles over stones behind Levin, and nobody can see where Sura is.
8. Kiaan notices that the scale grows warmer when he points it toward the peaks. So he holds it in both hands, so as not to lose the way, and leads them where it is warmest.
9. But Sura sees the children coming, beats her great grey wings and flies away to the highest peak, and the wind blows harder.
10. The way up that peak is loose stones that slide back with every step. Kiaan slips and nearly lets go of the scale, but he holds it tight in both hands while Max grabs his jacket and Levin pulls them all up.
11. At the top Sura turns her big head away when she sees the four children, and she lays one wing across the path like a wall, so the little ones cannot come to her.
12. Max calls "Sura, wait!", but she does not turn, and the wind is almost strong enough to lift her.
13. The only way past her wing is the last rock, too high for the three little ones. Kiaan presses the warm scale into Levin's hands. Levin is scared of the wind, but he climbs up, holds on tight and calls Sura's name into the autumn wind, louder than ever before.
14. Sura is afraid for the small boy alone on the high rock, and that fear is bigger than her shame, so she turns her head to him, and her chest turns toward the children too.
15. Julian sees a dark gap there where a scale is missing, with a tiny fire flickering behind it like a candle in the wind, and he shouts: "A scale is missing!"
16. Levin is now right beside her chest, and he presses the scale into the gap. Now the wind cannot get in, and the fire behind the scale grows big and warm.
17. With her fire warm again Sura is strong enough to hold herself on the rock, so she lifts Levin gently down with her nose and folds her wings to stay. Then she breathes a warm flame that lights the children's way back through the fog to the door in the old wall.
18. The four step out at the Grossmünster, the mist thins and the door in the old stone closes behind them, and they run home together across the Rathausbrücke in the evening, and Levin feels proud, because this time he called out loud all by himself.

Challenges taken:
1. The rising evening wind is the visible clock.
2. Levin's voice fails him; a loud call is needed.
3. Loose stones slide them back down the peak.
4. Sura must be persuaded to stay, not asked away.
5. A missing scale pressed back to block the wind.

items.planLine: close-up — Julian — Julian tucks the scale under his jacket against his tummy on the tram, chin down, arms crossed over it — Julian holds the scale and will not give it back; the scale is now kept warm against his body
items.arc:
1. Every autumn Saturday, Mama waits over by the Wasserkirche while Levin, Julian, Max and Kiaan visit the old dragon Funkenherz, who sleeps in the quiet corner beside the Grossmünster and flies off from any grown-up who comes near.
2. She lets them warm their cold hands at the golden scale over her heart, because her fire lives in it, and it must never go cold, she says.
3. But this Saturday that scale, as big as Levin's hand, lies on the autumn pavement, still warm, and Funkenherz beside the church wall is grey instead of red.
4. Levin wants to warn her that her fire has fallen out, but his voice comes out so small that Funkenherz, pretending all is well, flies off to the wooded hill by the zoo, where she goes when she wants to be alone among animals.
5. Because the scale is getting cooler in his hand, Levin asks Mama to take them to the zoo, and Mama rides the tram up the hill with all four.
6. On the tram the scale grows cooler still, so Julian, who remembers how Funkenherz warmed his cold hands, tucks it under his jacket against his warm tummy and will not give it back or let Levin go looking without him.
7. At the zoo, Mama waits on the bench by the flamingo pond, as she always waits by the Wasserkirche, and warns: "Stay away from the water, and stay together!"
8. So Kiaan, looking hard at the ground, spots huge claw prints in the wet leaves along the pond's edge.
9. But as they follow the prints, Julian slips, the scale slides out of his jacket toward the cold water, and Max leaps and catches it just in time, though it is colder now.
10. The prints lead away from the path into the fog between the trees, where a big grey rock opens one golden eye, and for the first time the children see that no warm steam rises from Funkenherz's back.
11. "I am only resting, go back to your Mama," she says with her face turned away, and because all four talk at once and Levin's voice stays small, she never hears about the scale.
12. Instead she flies slowly over the high zoo fence into the foggy wood, where no child can climb after her.
13. Now Funkenherz is gone in the fog, and under Julian's jacket only one tiny warm spot is left on the scale.
14. Twice Levin's small voice came too late, so he stretches out both arms and calls with his whole voice: "Funkenherz! Your heart-scale is here! Your fire is not gone!"
15. The big voice carries through the fog, and Funkenherz, who thought her fire was simply burning out with age, turns, glides back over the fence and lowers her chest to the children.
16. Julian's knees shake in front of the huge dragon, but he steps forward and presses the scale into the empty place over her heart.
17. The last spark jumps into her, her scales glow red again, and warm steam rises from her back.
18. Funkenherz curls her warm tail around all four, breathes warm air over their cold hands and says, "Thank you, Levin, for your big voice, and thank you, Julian, for keeping my fire warm," and Levin feels brave.

Challenges taken:
1. Funkenherz does not know her fire has fallen out.
2. She refuses the help the children bring.
3. Finding the hidden dragon among the zoo's trees and animals.
4. Small, slow Julian is not left behind.
5. Levin calls out loud although his voice is shy.

items.arc:
1. On an autumn afternoon Levin, his little brother Julian and their friends Max and Kiaan play ball on the Lindenhof, where the sun still shines on the Grossmünster towers across the roofs, and Kiaan wears his thick warm autumn jacket.
2. A man in an orange vest pushes his cart up onto the Lindenhof and starts his leaf blower, because he must get every leaf into the cart by the chess field before dark, so that nobody slips on them tomorrow.
3. When the ball rolls into the big leaf heap between the roots of a linden, Julian digs for it and finds an egg as big as a football and as warm as an oven tile, knocking softly from inside.
4. Nobody knows whose egg it is, but Julian spots a golden eye blinking in the linden's crown, and there, in her nest high in the branches, crouches a dragon as big as a horse, red and yellow exactly like the leaves.
5. Levin, who loves dragons, tells her their names, and she says she is Rubina: the cold wind from the lake shook her egg out of that nest, and it must be back in the warm nest before night, or her little one will never hatch.
6. But the linden is far too high for the children to climb, and Rubina cannot come down to them, because the roar hurts her fine ears, which are made to hear the faint knocking of her egg from far away, and with her wings pressed over her ears she cannot fly.
7. So the children pile leaves over the egg as a blanket, and Levin goes to ask the man to stop, but the blower swallows his whisper, and when the man switches off, says he is Herr Keller and asks "What?", Levin turns red and says nothing.
8. In that short quiet Julian sees Rubina climb down the trunk with her branch-claws toward the egg, but when Max shouts into Herr Keller's ear that a dragon egg lies under the leaves, Herr Keller laughs that dragons live only in books and switches on again, and Rubina climbs back up into the crown.
9. The blast blows the leaf blanket away, so the egg wobbles out of the roots and rolls down the slope toward the steep stairs.
10. Levin shouts "Careful, stairs!", and Max runs as fast as he can and stops the egg with his foot like a football, right at the top step.
11. Kiaan pulls off his warm jacket, wraps the egg in it and carries it carefully back under the linden, but the wind is cold and the knocking grows quieter.
12. Soon the sun lights only the tips of the Grossmünster towers, Herr Keller roars up to blow away the last leaves right under the linden, and inside the jacket the knocking almost stops.
13. But Julian remembers: "When it was quiet, Rubina came down!"
14. Levin saw that Herr Keller switches off for anyone who tugs his sleeve, so with shaking knees he tugs it and asks loudly how the leaf blower works.
15. Herr Keller switches off and turns to show him the cart by the chess field, his back to the linden, and Levin asks question after question: twice Herr Keller reaches for the switch, and twice Levin asks something new.
16. Rubina climbs down the trunk, a branch cracks and Herr Keller half turns, so she presses flat against the bark until Levin quickly asks how heavy the full cart is, and then she climbs the last bit and holds out claws that are made for branches and cannot grip the egg off the ground, so Kiaan lifts it up to her in his jacket.
17. She breathes warm air over the egg and carries it up into the nest, leaving the jacket in Kiaan's hands, and her wing beats shake every last leaf off the linden, so that Herr Keller turns round and sees his clean square covered red and yellow in the dusk and groans that he must start all over tomorrow.
18. Up in the warm nest the egg cracks and a little dragon peeks out at the four friends, and Rubina climbs down once more, says "Thank you!" and breathes a warm puff onto their cold hands, Julian strokes her nose, and Levin beams: "This time I dared!"

Challenges taken:
1. daylight running out over the Lindenhof
2. the egg must be home before dark
3. the fragile egg rolls toward the steep stairs
4. Kiaan holds the egg up into a dragon's claws
5. Rubina freezes on the trunk as Herr Keller half turns

items.planLine: wide — the harbour of Peschero, the «Goldene Möwe» at the quay, no people in frame — the ship rests in summer morning light with her name on the hull — the world and the ship are established before anyone steps aboard
items.arc:
1. High summer in the harbour of Peschero: Fiona spreads out the treasure map of Insel Cardo, whose torn edge cuts off the shallow water, and Lorena, who has read tide lines since she was small, pencils the shallow marks in crooked along the sandbanks; Fiona says that on the «Goldene Möwe» the captain draws and the captain steers, takes the pencil out of her hand and redraws the line straight and neat, therefore Lorena's crooked mark is gone. Lorena shuts her mouth and is angry.

2. Facundo rolls the last barrel across his cluttered deck and says it out loud: "We can't outsail the «Schwarze Nadel», so we take the sandbanks — she draws too deep to follow us there, and whoever comes last comes home with nothing." Sarah comes back from the quay full of harbour talk: the old watchtower on Cardo belongs to Rossa's family, an old sea drain runs from under it down into the lagoon, and nobody has carried that chest home for two generations.

3. Saira jumps onto the rail and shouts that she will go down any hole on that island first; Rossa hears the whole plan from her own quay, tells Fiona flatly that her grandfather went under that tower and came up with nothing but stories, therefore she means to bring the chest up herself, and she sails into the deep channel one hour ahead. Fiona stays cheerful, because the banks are her own idea.

4. On the sandbanks the tide falls faster than Fiona's straightened line promised, therefore the Möwe sits fast in the sand; Lorena says three times that her crooked line was the right one, but the five of them dig with buckets for two hours and the sand slides back faster than they lift it, so the trench ends exactly where it began. Fiona is ashamed and does not look at Lorena.

5. Fiona stops the digging and invents a second way: they hang the spare sail under the hull and swing their whole weight out on the boom until the ship heels over and slides across on her side, so the Möwe comes free at dusk — but the spare sail comes up in rags, therefore the ship now carries no second canvas at all.

6. In the night a young gull tangled in fishing line thumps onto the deck; Lorena decides to keep it and works the line off its wing, Sarah names it Krümel because it eats crumbs out of her palm and answers everything she says, therefore Lorena promises it a share of her supper every day.

7. At noon Cardo lies in the heat with the «Schwarze Nadel» anchored in the lagoon and Rossa's flag stuck in the beach; Fiona looks at the Nadel's deep hull and at the wet tide scar high on the lagoon rock and warns Rossa that the lagoon runs dry by evening, but Rossa answers, "I anchor where I want." Fiona feels the race is over before it started.

8. Rossa tells them her own crew went down the shaft at dawn, lost the way in the forked passages, burned the lamp out and came back with empty hands, therefore she will stand at the mouth and wait for whoever is fool enough to carry it up; Fiona climbs down anyway, because she has seen the tide scar and says quietly to her crew that Rossa can hold the chest tonight but cannot sail with it.

9. Saira goes first because she is never afraid, but at the fork she cannot choose between the two openings and stands still until a quarter of the lamp oil has burned; Fiona chalks every corner so the way back can be walked exactly, takes the left passage, and they find the iron chest in the old cistern.

10. Facundo ropes the chest up the shaft on his own, but at the mouth Rossa's crew lifts it away before anybody has climbed out, and Rossa says the chest belongs above her grandfather's tower and not in a stranger's hold, therefore she rolls a stone over the shaft mouth with all five of them still below. Fiona is frightened for the first time on this voyage.

11. In the sealed dark the lamp burns low; Sarah keeps talking — about her aunt's crooked kitchen in Peschero, about Krümel, about the price of rope — therefore nobody loses their head and they walk the chalk marks back to the cistern, where Fiona says out loud that she has no plan left.

12. Saira remembers Sarah's harbour talk about the sea drain, holds her wet hand along the cistern wall until she feels warm air moving, and for once decides without dithering: she digs the packed sand and stones out of the low opening until it is wide enough, but the lamp falls into the water and goes out, therefore the last stretch of the crawl is done blind.

13. They come out into the lagoon at dusk on hands and knees and find the water drained, the hot summer wind drifting sand across the entrance, and the «Schwarze Nadel» lying over on her deep keel with the chest on her deck; Rossa stands on the rail and says, "You know how to lay a ship over." She does not ask nicely, and she offers nothing.

14. Fiona names her price out loud — half of the chest — and does not lower it while the light goes; Rossa refuses twice and the crews sit on the sand, but the wind keeps pushing sand into the entrance, therefore Rossa says yes. Fiona is calm, though the work will cost them the night tide over the banks.

15. Both crews hang the Nadel's own spare sail under her hull and swing out on the boom the way the Möwe was freed that morning, Saira throwing her whole weight onto the end of it, so the Nadel rolls over and slides free while that sail tears to rags too; the chest is opened on the sand between the two ships and holds gold coins, a gold compass rose, and the logbook of two captains who reached this treasure and lost their ships on the banks going home, therefore Rossa counts out half with a closed face, and Fiona reads the logbook twice and tells Lorena she is sorry about the pencil.

16. At dawn Fiona waits for the tide, puts Lorena at the wheel and stands back with empty hands; Lorena reads the true tide line and takes the «Goldene Möwe» over the sandbanks clean, therefore Fiona laughs out loud with Krümel screeching on the mast, glad, and not once wanting to correct anything.

Challenges taken:
1. The «Goldene Möwe» grounded on the falling tide.
2. The chest taken at the shaft mouth and the crew sealed underground.
3. Freeing the rival's ship on Fiona's terms.

items.planLine: ultra-wide — the harbour of Calamora, the «Goldene Möwe» at the dock, no people in frame — the old sea chart lies unrolled on the empty deck, one finger-worn island circled at its centre — the destination Cadura and the quest are established before anyone speaks
items.arc:
1. It is high summer in the harbour of Calamora, and Kapitänin Fiona spreads an old sea chart on the deck of the «Goldene Möwe». She points at the island Cadura and says, "Two generations, and nobody has lifted it. We will." Fiona is eager, because she has wanted her own crew's name on a find like this since she first took the wheel.

2. Lorena comes up from below with a coil of rope over her shoulder and states the rule flatly: "The crew that lifts the treasure first keeps it. The other sails home with empty hands. Rossa's «Sturmnadel» has the same chart and she is faster, so we leave before sunrise."

3. But Fiona copies the coastline three times, because the bays on her drawing are never neat enough; therefore the «Goldene Möwe» leaves three hours late, and Rossa calls across from her passing deck, "I'll keep you a place, Fiona — in the harbour." Fiona is ashamed of the lost hours, but she says the chart had to be right.

4. On the second day fog closes over the sea, and Saira at the wheel cannot pick a channel: "East? West? East — no. Wait." Facundo digs through the gear he left heaped on deck and shouts, "The compass is under here somewhere, I swear it!" He does not find it, therefore the ship drifts.

5. Sarah stands at the bow and talks without stopping — about biscuits, about her aunt, about the colour of nothing — so that Lorena at the wheel always knows where the bow is in the fog. They stay off the rocks, but the swell tears the ship's boat from its ropes and smashes it, and a whole night is lost.

6. At first light Saira chooses the western channel because the current there runs stronger, and she steers them out; therefore they reach Cadura, but the «Sturmnadel» already lies in the only bay and Rossa's crew is digging in the cave, the one sheltered place a chest could sit. Fiona is afraid the race is already over.

7. Because the boat is gone and the bay is taken, Facundo swims a line to the rocks and the crew hauls itself through the surf on rope and canvas. Everything they carry is soaked, so they come ashore with a plank, a coil of rope and nothing else.

8. On the sand Sarah tells her own crew about the shelf of rock she can see high on the cliff and the overhang above it. Rossa hears her from the cave mouth, therefore Rossa's people leave the cave and set a ladder against the cliff.

9. Halfway up the rock a grey parrot lands on Lorena's arm. Sarah feeds it a ship's biscuit, so they name it Zwieback there on the ledge, and the bird repeats one cracked sentence: "Under the fig tree."

10. A wooden chest stands on the ledge, but Facundo's rope is knotted into a tangle and the first sling slips. Fiona cuts the mainsail and makes a wide canvas sling instead, therefore the chest comes down whole — and the «Goldene Möwe» has lost her big sail.

11. At the foot of the cliff they open the chest: no gold, only the logbook of the crew that hid the treasure, and the last page records that they sailed away and left their grey parrot behind on Cadura. Fiona is disappointed, because the book names no place at all.

12. Zwieback flies back up to the ledge every time they turn to go; Lorena wavers, then refuses to leave the bird alone. The coaxing costs exactly the minutes Rossa needs to reach the foot of the cliff, and Rossa takes the chest and the logbook out of Fiona's hands: "Found on my beach. Mine." Fiona asks for the book once and Rossa says no.

13. Fiona has read the page and heard the bird, therefore she does not ask twice and does not stop to draw a clean chart. She scratches three crooked lines into the dust, points up the slope and says one word: "Fig tree." They run and leave the chest and the logbook with Rossa, and Fiona is angry about the book, but she runs.

14. Zwieback flies ahead to the old fig tree above the bay, Saira sprints after it without pausing once, and Facundo digs with the plank and both hands until a heavy sack of coins comes out of the dry earth. But Rossa drops the chest on the sand and climbs the slope behind them.

15. Rossa reaches the pit as the sack lifts clear, sees the coins already in Fiona's hands and the hole already open, and by the rule between crews she has nothing left to claim; she carries the logbook back down and rows out to the «Sturmnadel» empty-handed, and Fiona is sorry for her but keeps the sack. Then Saira lashes the canvas sling to the planks of the smashed boat, Facundo swims the line, and the crew tows the gold out through the surf.

16. The «Goldene Möwe» sails home slowly under a sail patched crooked out of canvas scraps. Zwieback sits on Fiona's shoulder and says "Under the fig tree" until the whole crew is laughing, and Fiona is proud of her crooked sail.

Challenges taken:
1. A late start and a fog crossing that costs the boat and a night.
2. Landing second, with the only bay held, and getting the chest off the cliff.
3. Losing the chest and logbook to Rossa, and reaching the fig tree first anyway.

items.planLine: close-up — the big raven standing over the nest, wings spread wide, both half-scales beneath it — the raven spreads its wings over the nest — both halves are taken and the boys have nothing
items.arc:
1. On a hot summer morning Levin rings the silver bell on his handlebar at the Lindenhof and tells Julian that today they will find a real dragon, because he has read about dragons all summer; Julian packs his ball and his bread roll into his rucksack, because he never rides without both.
2. At the fountain they meet Max with his dog Nia and Kiaan; Max shouts that Nia can smell a sausage from the far bank, but Kiaan reads the hill's name off the signpost and says quietly that he will ride the valley loop with them.
3. On the gravel road out of the city the bell shakes loose and drops, therefore Levin, who often drops things, picks it up and puts it in his trouser pocket; a raven lands on a fence post and watches the bell until the boys ride on.
4. They lean the bicycles against a fir tree above the valley, and in the grass at the mouth of a cave Levin finds half a silver scale with a jagged broken edge.
5. A dragon steps out of the cave with the mist, one wing bare and grey; he beats the wing once, drops back onto the stones, and says slowly, "I cannot fly, so I cannot get home over the ridge tonight." Julian hides behind Levin, then holds out one piece of his bread, and because the dragon came with the mist the boys call him Nebel.
6. Nebel says two ravens dragged the scale off in the night and cracked it, so one half fell here and the other lies in their nest on the next summit, where they keep everything that shines; therefore Levin says, "We must fetch the other half, or Nebel sleeps out here alone," and Julian says, "Only if you walk in front."
7. Nia pulls Max and Kiaan up off the lower path because she smells the scale in Levin's hand, and Max says Nia found it first and will find the rest too, so the four boys climb on together.
8. Higher up the path forks into three ways that all end at the summit gate, and from the fork they can see Nebel far below beating his wing and falling back again; Levin takes the short middle way with Julian because Julian's legs are slow, but the middle way is the one with water on it.
9. The middle way ends at a fast cold brook, therefore Levin wades in first and slips at once; Julian throws him the ball, Levin holds it and reaches the far bank, but the current carries the ball away downstream and Julian says nothing for a long time.
10. Julian will not put one foot in the water, so Levin wades back and carries him across at the shallow bend, and the two crossings cost them the whole afternoon.
11. They reach the summit gate last, with the sun already low; Kiaan reads the weathered post aloud, letter by letter: the ravens above take what shines and give nothing back.
12. An iron bar has rusted tight against the gate, therefore Nia digs the packed earth out from under it, Max lifts with both arms, and all four push until the gate scrapes open; their arms hurt and Kiaan says he has forgotten his water.
13. On the summit two ravens sit on a heap of shiny things: the big one talks without stopping about everything the mountain has given them, and the small one only says, "No."
14. Levin holds out the jagged half and explains that it belongs to Nebel, but the big raven snatches it out of his hand, drops both halves into the nest, and stands over the nest with its wings spread wide.
15. Julian cries, Levin sits down on a stone, and the sun goes behind the ridge, because now the boys have nothing at all and Nebel cannot go home.
16. Then Levin remembers the raven on the fence post that watched his bell, therefore he takes the bell from his pocket, rings it, and sets it on a flat stone; both ravens leave the nest for the new shiny sound and squabble over it.
17. Julian is small and quiet, so he walks to the nest alone, lifts out the second half, and carries it back; the jagged edges click together in Levin's hands, and Levin says Julian did that part by himself.
18. They run down in the last light and Nebel presses the whole scale into the bare patch, where the ridges lock and the wing beats; he carries the four boys once over the Grossmünster and the Limmat, and the big raven flies alongside, sees the mended wing, screams once, and turns back to its ringing bell — later, riding home, Levin's handlebar is empty, but he stops, hears the ringing far up on the mountain, and grins.

Challenges taken:
1. The brook on the short way — ball lost, Julian carried, time gone.
2. The jammed summit gate — dug, lifted, pushed together, late and aching.
3. The ravens take both halves and guard the nest — low point.
4. Levin trades the bell; Julian fetches the half alone.

items.planLine: ultra-wide — the castle bank in darkness — every lantern on the far bank is out, one small glow where Ethan holds his coat closed, the warm lights of the adults unreachable across the fog — the children are stranded on the dark bank with one flame and no matches
items.arc:
1. It is the autumn holidays in Baden, and from the window of the new flat under the Stadtturm Lily watches children carry turnip lanterns up the lane to practise for the walk on the last evening; a boy at the front carries his lantern on a long pole. At supper Ethan says that if they know nobody by Monday they will walk back through the school gates as alone as they left, therefore they are going on that walk.

2. They run down to the lane, and Lily says straight out that she and her brother want to walk at the front too. The boy answers that the line is full and that the front is his, because he led it last year. Ethan opens his mouth and no sound comes out, so the boy goes back to his practice. Both children feel small.

3. In the morning Rachel says that anybody with a lantern may walk, even at the very back, therefore they need lanterns. They cross the Holzbrücke to the market with Margaret, who touches each roof post as she counts them aloud. At the crate James turns over what is left and says both turnips are small and soft.

4. The hollowing scoop is a heavy grown-up thing, and it tears straight through the side of Lily's turnip. Lily is angry with herself. Ethan hollows both turnips instead and tapes the torn side shut, but the work takes the whole afternoon, so they buy the candles in the last shop still open.

5. In the Kurpark Lily fits one candle into her taped lantern and sets the box down on the bench, but Ethan is impatient to see the lane again and hurries her away without it. When they run back at dusk the bench is empty. They have one candle between them, and it is standing in the mended turnip.

6. On the last evening Ethan strikes Rachel's match, lights the candle himself and leaves the matchbox lying on the kitchen table. At the fountain the boy lifts his pole and tells them that if they must come they will walk behind everybody. Lily is happy anyway, because they are in the walk.

7. The boy sets a fast pace to be first over the bridge. A small girl from Lily's class calls out that she cannot keep up and begins to cry, but the boy does not slacken. Lily's legs are too short as well, so Ethan stays beside her, and the two of them are last onto the Holzbrücke.

8. Fog comes off the Limmat and fills the bridge until neither end can be seen. Lily is frightened and wants to run, so Ethan makes her count the roof posts the way Margaret counted them. He holds the lantern inside his coat, out of the wind, all the way across.

9. On the castle bank the wind takes lantern after lantern until every one of them is out, including the boy's on its pole. The grown-ups are still on the Altstadt side; the children can see the lights where the hot punch is being poured, and they cannot reach it through the fog. Ethan remembers the matchbox on the kitchen table.

10. Ethan opens his coat, and their candle is the only flame left. He holds it out to the boy, but the boy says he takes no light from someone who is not in his line, and turns his back. Ethan is angry, and again he says nothing.

11. The small girl from Lily's class is crying in the dark. Lily is frightened of the flame, but she carries the lantern to the boy herself, tells him that nobody can see and that he is the one at the front, and stands still while he opens his lantern and dips his candle down to her stub.

12. One lantern is lit from the boy's, then another from that one, until the whole line is burning again. The little ones will not walk anywhere except beside Lily's lantern, so the boy comes back from the front and walks the whole way home beside her.

13. The stub gutters out on the last steps up into the Altstadt, by which time every other lantern is lit. At their door Ethan finds his voice, tells the boy his name and points up at the window under the Stadtturm, and the boy says he will knock for them at eight.

14. On Monday Lily lets go of Margaret's hand at the school gate and walks in by herself, and the girl from the walk calls her across the yard. Afterwards she tells Ethan that her coat still smells of burnt turnip, and that she likes it.

Challenges taken:
1. Getting lanterns at all after the boy refuses them.
2. One candle left, and starting last behind a boy who will not slow down.
3. A dark bank, no matches, and a boy who will not take their light.

items.arc:
1. In high summer the pirate ship «Goldene Möwe» still lies at the quay of the harbour town Cala Fenice at noon, because Captain Fiona has been copying her treasure map below deck since sunrise and says the one finished copy is still not clean enough to sail with.
2. Saira swings down the ladder and says it straight: "Evening wind or nothing — Rossa's «Sturmnadel» is faster, and whoever touches that island second goes home with empty hands." Fiona rolls up the copy and feels caught out, therefore she agrees to sail.
3. But nobody aboard knows when the water at the island's reef gate stands still, so Fiona sends Sarah and Lorena to the fountain where the net menders sit; Sarah asks about "just a little fishing trip out to the flat water, nothing special, we like flat water, my aunt liked flat water too" and talks so long that she nearly says the island's name, until Lorena steps on her foot and says nothing at all.
4. The net menders read the tides of the whole gulf, but they want payment, therefore Fiona hands over her brass spyglass and learns that the outer water runs hard out to sea all day and stands still for one hour before sunrise.
5. Rossa is filling her water casks at the same fountain and has heard the words "flat water" and "before sunrise"; she comes down the quay and says, "My grandmother's crew found that chest, locked their own compass inside it, swore to come back for it and died old at home — I will not," then she casts off first.
6. Facundo shouts that he can walk the anchor up alone, but his heaped ropes have jammed the anchor line, so the crew loses the last daylight picking the knot apart; Facundo is ashamed and coils every rope on deck before he sleeps.
7. They come to the reef gate in the dark, and now the spyglass is gone, therefore nobody can read where the rocks stand in the white water; Saira says maybe wait, maybe risk it, maybe wait, and Lorena says flatly that she is not turning for home.
8. Fiona is certain the race is lost, therefore she takes the small boat out on a line to feel for a way through, but the current spins the boat sideways, Facundo hauls her back aboard by the rope, and the boat is torn away and gone; Fiona sits on deck, wet and frightened, and says the boat was her fault.
9. An hour later the lanterns of the «Sturmnadel» drive straight through the gate under full sail, because Rossa knows from the fountain that the still water comes at dawn and will not leave it to anyone else; Fiona watches the lanterns disappear and does not speak.
10. In the long dark hour Saira says they should turn back before they lose more, Sarah makes a joke about swimming home and nobody laughs, Lorena refuses to move from the rail, and Fiona finally says that she will get them in even if they arrive last and even if nothing about it is neat — therefore the crew stays.
11. At the still hour before sunrise they sail the gate cleanly, but without the boat they must wade the last stretch ashore, and they follow the booming of the sea cave and a sound of hammering to a chamber behind a low neck of rock.
12. Inside, the chest sits under a fallen roof slab: the old crew lowered it through a hole above, the rock came down afterwards, so the lid cannot lift and the chest is wider than the neck; Rossa is hammering at the neck to widen it and does not step aside for anyone.
13. Sarah talks and talks until Rossa admits she has hammered all night for one hand's width of stone; Fiona looks at the low slab and sees that the chest can be tipped onto its side, because then the lid swings open toward the neck — but a tipped chest wedges and can never be dragged out whole, therefore Rossa says no.
14. The water climbs to their knees, so Fiona says half the coin is Rossa's whether she helps or not, and Facundo, Lorena and Saira put their shoulders under the chest and tip it while Rossa stands and watches her grandmother's chest wedge into the rock for ever; the lid falls open, Fiona rolls her one finished copy into a chute, and both crews pour coin through the neck sack by sack while the ink runs off the paper.
15. With no small boat they can only wade out what they can carry, therefore both crews leave the rest of the coin to the rising tide; on the beach Rossa says, "The second crew goes home empty — that has been true for two generations," and Fiona takes the old compass with the scratched names out of the last sack and puts it in her hand.
16. The «Goldene Möwe» sails north with heavy sacks below deck and a sheet of ruined paper drying on the rail, and Fiona laughs out loud in the sun, because not one line of this voyage was drawn straight.

Challenges taken:
1. Buying the tide without telling the rival — costs the spyglass.
2. The reef gate in the dark, blind — costs the small boat and the night.
3. The chest that will not fit the neck, held by a captain who will not tip it — costs the chest, the map and most of the coin.

items.arc:
1. On a summer morning Levin rides with Julian, Max and Kiaan to the old earth walls on the Uetliberg, because Levin wants to find dragon bones there; Max shouts "Hoi!" over the rampart and the valley shouts it back, but Levin is too shy to shout, and grey cloud lies far away on the Alps.
2. Julian sits down to eat, feels something warm under the leaves and digs out a speckled egg that hums in his hands; Kiaan lifts a black feather from the moss beside it and says quietly, "A bird carried this here."
3. The egg glows, cracks, and a small wet dragon climbs out and sneezes at four faces; he says only "Mami. Bärg. Nacht", then points with his snout at the far mountains and at the sun.
4. The boys decide to help him, therefore they name him Fünkli, and Levin says out loud, "Fünkli must get high up before the sun goes down, or he stays alone in the dark."
5. Levin chooses the lookout tower, because it is the highest place they are allowed to climb; the path is too steep for bikes, therefore they push the bikes back to the rampart and go on foot.
6. Julian puts the shiniest piece of eggshell in his pocket, because it is the only thing Fünkli has from home; a big raven watches from a beech, because the shining thing it stole from the mountains is broken open now, and it follows them.
7. At midday a deep rumble rolls down from the mountains and Max says, "That's thunder, for sure!", but Fünkli lifts his head and hums back at it.
8. The grey cloud brings rain and fills Fünkli's wings, therefore the boys carry him in turns and get slow; Levin slips on a wet root and drops him into the ferns, so Fünkli is frightened and refuses to walk one more step.
9. Julian holds out his last Weggli, therefore Fünkli eats it and waddles after him, but Julian is hungry for the whole rest of the day.
10. A storm-fallen beech lies across the path, so they must cross the open meadow; Kiaan stands still and waits until he sees where the deer slip through, and the waiting costs them a long time, which makes Levin worried about the sun.
11. In the open Max holds the shell up and calls, "Look how it shines!", therefore the raven dives at them again and again until they hide in the bushes and lose the last light; Max says he is sorry, and Julian hides the shell under his jacket.
12. Fünkli is too tired for the tower steps, therefore Levin carries him up while Kiaan counts every step out loud, and the counting keeps hungry Julian climbing; near the top Kiaan points at the raven's nest of shiny things under the roof.
13. On the platform the sun is sitting on the peaks, so Max uncovers the shell and flashes it at the mountains, because nothing else is left to try; nothing answers, but the raven sees the gleam and snatches the shell out of his hand.
14. Then the sun is gone, the mountains are black, Fünkli's light is only a spark, and he cries against Levin's chest at the railing; Levin feels that it is his fault, because the tower was his plan.
15. Levin remembers the morning at the rampart, when the valley shouted back — therefore the mountains do not have to see Fünkli, they have to hear him — so Levin, who did not dare answer the echo, shouts as loud as he can and tells the others to shout with him.
16. Four boys roar with Fünkli's small deep call over the dark valley, past the red lights of the television tower; the roar startles the raven above them, so the shell drops, and Julian catches it with both hands.
17. Far away the rumble answers, and it is not thunder: a wide shadow lands on the roof, the raven flaps back to its empty nest, and Fünkli's mother lifts her son in her claws, because his wings are still wet.
18. Julian presses the shell into Fünkli's paw, Fünkli lays his warm head against Levin's cheek, and later, pushing his bike home through the dark, Levin calls "Gute Nacht, Fünkli!" so loudly that the whole valley says it after him.

Challenges taken:
1. Rain soaks Fünkli's wings; he is heavy and then refuses to walk.
2. A fallen beech forces the open meadow; the raven attacks and the last light is lost.
3. The light signal from the tower fails; the raven takes the eggshell.
4. Full dark, no answer, Fünkli's glow only a spark.

items.arc:
1. On a summer morning Levin and Julian stand with their bikes on the Rathausbrücke over the Limmat, and Levin shows Julian the new lamp on his handlebar, because he does not like the dark and the lamp is the best thing he owns; Julian puts a roll in his pocket; Mama says one thing: be back at this bridge before the streetlights come on, she will wait here.
2. They ride out of the city and push their bikes up the Farnberg, where the path ends at a cave mouth; Levin leans his bike on a rock and leaves the lamp clipped to the handlebar, because Julian reminds him that he forgets whatever he carries.
3. In the moss at the cave mouth Levin picks up a small golden scale, and he says it is warm, warmer than a stone in the sun; he lets Julian feel it too.
4. A dragon comes out of the cave, so big that his shoulder fills the entrance, and there is a gap in his right wing; Julian is frightened and hides behind Levin, but then he peeks out and says hello, and the dragon says his name is Fenno and that the little scale chipped off his big wing scale when it hit the ground this morning.
5. Nia comes up the path with Max and Kiaan pushing their bikes behind her; Max says she turned off the lake road and would not stop for anything, and Kiaan kneels down and whispers that until today he had only read about dragons.
6. Fenno tells all four that a Bergmännli called Nolo snatched the big scale here at his own cave mouth and carried it up the Zwirbelspitz, therefore he cannot fly home to his family tonight; he says he is ashamed to ask children.
7. Levin says it out loud: "We bring the scale back before the streetlights come on, and nobody walks alone"; at the fork Kiaan reads Zwirbelspitz on the signpost while Nia pulls up the middle path, but the ridge is long, so the climb eats the whole afternoon.
8. On the summit Nolo sits in a hole between the rocks, a small grey Bergmännli with the big scale under his chin, and he says he found it, therefore it is his; his lantern stone cracked years ago, so this is the brightest thing left on his mountain.
9. Kiaan asks him politely and Julian holds out his roll, but Max shouts that the scale belongs to a dragon; therefore Nolo drags a stone slab over his hole and says nothing more, and Levin has no idea left.
10. Down at the cave Fenno lies flat and says they should go home, but Levin looks at the lamp on his handlebar and says Nolo does not want gold, he wants light; therefore Levin unclips the lamp, although it is the only thing that would get him home in the dark.
11. They climb the Zwirbelspitz a second time, their legs burn, and the sun goes down behind the Uetliberg; Levin knocks on the slab and clicks the lamp on.
12. Nolo grabs for the lamp, but Levin sets it down on the stone, steps back out of reach and says nobody will take it back; therefore Nolo clicks the button twice and pushes the big scale across to him.
13. Nolo follows them down the slope, because he says they will grab his lamp back as soon as it is properly dark; on the loose scree Levin stumbles, therefore the big scale slips out of his hands and slides deep between the stones.
14. Nolo says lost is lost, tomorrow he will dig it out and it will be his again, therefore he will not shine his lamp for boys who want it back; Levin says straight out that he dropped it and that it is his fault, and nobody shouts at him, but Julian cries and Levin is afraid of the dark.
15. Then Levin remembers how the little scale felt in his hand in the morning, so he crawls over the scree and lays both palms on stone after stone until one stone is warm; he pulls the big scale out from under it, and Nolo stands three steps away and says nothing.
16. At the cave Levin presses the scale into the gap and Fenno's wing closes and lifts him off the ground; Nolo watches from the cave mouth, then clicks his lamp on and climbs down into his tunnels with it.
17. Fenno kneels so the four boys and Nia can climb on, therefore they ride once over Zurich, past the towers of the Grossmünster and along the Limmat, and he sets them down at the Rathausbrücke, where Mama is waiting under the lit streetlights and Levin tells her at once that he is late and that his lamp is gone for good.
18. Mama pulls him close and says she saw a big shadow cross the water; Fenno lifts off and turns toward his own mountains, and the four boys ride home together through the dark streets, and Levin is not afraid of the dark, because he found the scale in it with his own hands.

Challenges taken:
1. Nolo refuses and shuts himself in.
2. Levin gives up his lamp and climbs twice.
3. The scale is lost in the dark, and the light is Nolo's.
4. Coming home late with no light.

items.arc:
1. On a grey autumn Saturday Levin says he wants to see something nobody in his class has ever seen, so he and Julian ride past the Grossmünster and up the Uetliberg, with Julian's ball in the backpack.
2. High up under the television tower Julian finds a scale as big as his hand in the wet leaves, and it is warm; behind the bushes Levin notices a cave where the leaves are dry and warm air comes out, although the whole mountain is wet.
3. A dragon steps out of the cave and drags one wing over the stones; Levin is too shy to say a word, so Julian asks him what is wrong.
4. The dragon says the big scale is missing from his wing, so he cannot fly, and Julian's warm scale is only a small one he shed while waiting here; the big one fell last spring on the next summit, where he slipped and broke the roof of a marmot burrow, and the two marmots there keep it.
5. Nia comes up the path towing Max and Kiaan, and Max says she caught a warm smell at the first bench and has pulled them uphill ever since; Kiaan opens his animal book and reads that a marmot must have a dry burrow or it cannot sleep through the winter.
6. The dragon says his family waits beyond a mountain pass that closes with the first snow, therefore he asks the boys to fetch the scale; Levin knows at once that they must go, but he is too shy to answer, so nobody answers.
7. The dragon starts up the rocky slope himself, but the dragging wing catches on a stone and he slides back down to the cave; then Max says they all go together, because the dragon cannot climb, and Levin nods and says he will call him Bimo.
8. They lean their bikes against the rock by the cave and climb on, until a brown brook cuts the path, loud and fast, and Julian throws his ball in: it shoots away down the middle where the water is deep.
9. Beside the big flat stones the bottom shows, so they wade across there, but the ball does not come back and Julian cries.
10. On the summit there is nothing but stones and holes, so Levin holds the little shed scale under Nia's nose, and at one hole she digs and barks.
11. Two marmots pop out: Pfiff whistles short and sharp, and old Rösi says the dragon broke their roof in spring, so his big scale is now the only door that keeps the wet out — while she speaks, sleet drips through the crack onto her back.
12. Max shouts that they are thieves, so Rösi says that is rude, and both marmots drop down and plug the hole with the scale from inside.
13. The boys scratch at the stony ground, but the hole stays shut, the sleet turns to snow, and Julian says he wants to go home now.
14. Then Levin remembers the dry leaves and the warm air at the cave and what Kiaan read, and for the first time he speaks up by himself: he kneels at the plugged hole and offers the marmots Bimo's cave, because Bimo is flying home and it will stand warm and empty all winter.
15. Rösi pushes up with the scale in her paws, because she will not leave her door behind, and says she will look at that cave before she believes anything; she follows the boys down with Pfiff running ahead, and inside she lies flat on the dry warm floor.
16. Bimo says he is sorry that he broke her roof in spring, and Rösi holds the big scale out to Levin.
17. Levin presses the scale into the empty place in the wing himself, and Bimo carries the four boys and Nia once over Zurich, over the glass roof of the main station and the two towers of the Grossmünster.
18. Bimo sets them down beside their bikes and flies off towards the pass; Levin shouts goodbye after him, loud and by himself, and watches until the dragon is only a dot.

Challenges taken:
1. Levin too shy to answer the dragon.
2. The fast brown brook.
3. Hundreds of holes on the stony summit.
4. The marmots refuse and seal the scale in.

items.arc:
1. On a windy autumn afternoon Fiona sits at her kitchen table in Zurich and copies a torn old chart onto clean paper, because the chest that chart shows is on no map any more; she tells Sarah that they must reach it before next week's storms shut the sea. Sarah leans over her shoulder and names the marks she has heard Fiona describe a hundred times: three rocks, a black cove, a shelf of sand. Fiona says the rest is only her memory, therefore the map has to be perfect. Rain stands on the window above the towers of the Grossmünster.

2. Saira and Lorena come up the stairs with the costume bag. Lorena says, short and flat, that she is not going home without that chest, so she pulls her boots on first. Saira cannot choose between two hats, therefore she wears both. Facundo arrives last and drops his sword, his belt and his wet boots in the middle of the kitchen floor.

3. Fiona spreads the map wide on the table. The window bangs open, the autumn wind pours through, and in the next moment all five stand in pirate coats on the deck of the Sturmfeder with the grey sea rolling under them. Lorena points ahead at a rusty chain lying across a harbour mouth and says the name: Krummhafen, the town that lets no stranger through.

4. A black rowing boat comes out from under the chain. Hafenmeisterin Malva Grimm rows twice around the ship and looks far longer at the map in Fiona's hands than at the crew, therefore Fiona holds it flat against her coat. Malva says she has hunted that same chest for eleven years with a chart torn in half, so she will lift the chain this minute if Fiona hands the map down. Fiona feels her stomach go cold, but she says no.

5. Malva does not argue. She says the chain lifts only for a crew this town owes something, then she rows the five to the quay herself, because she is sure they will fail and come back to her offer. On the quay the dockworkers crowd round and shout that the crane has stood dead for a year and that they are carrying the salt aboard by hand before the storms.

6. Facundo lifts the heavy iron hook with both arms, but it slips straight out of the old chain ring. Fiona looks at the two parts and does not dare begin, because whatever she builds will not look right. Saira cannot decide between rope and wood, until Sarah jokes that a pirate is allowed to try both before supper — therefore Saira laughs and fetches both.

7. Fiona carves a wedge out of a barrel stave and drives it in beside the hook, so the hook cannot slip out of the ring again. The crane swings salt barrels aboard until dark and the whole quay cheers, but the work has eaten a full day of the good weather. With her own dockworkers cheering around her, Malva must give this crew the harbour; she says the chain comes down at first light and not one minute sooner.

8. Fiona hands the map to Facundo and asks him to lock it in the chart box, but fiddles start on the quay, so he sets it down on the deck and climbs back ashore. In the dusk Malva's two rowers come alongside the empty ship and lift the map off the planks. Sarah sees a boat pull away from the Sturmfeder, but she thinks it is a fisherman, therefore she says nothing.

9. At first light the dockworkers lower the chain, but Malva's berth is empty: the Eisenmöwe sailed in the night with the map, hours ahead of them. Facundo says out loud that it is his fault. Fiona is not angry with Facundo, she is angry with herself, and she says they should turn back, because she cannot draw a chart she knows will be wrong.

10. Lorena plants herself against the mast and refuses to move the ship one metre towards home. Sarah talks for a whole hour about every line Fiona ever showed her, so the three rocks, the black cove and the shelf of sand come back one by one. Fiona takes charcoal and draws them on a piece of sailcloth; the drawing is crooked and smudged and she is ashamed of it, but she pins it to the mast.

11. They sail by that sailcloth into cold fog, which burns their last lantern oil and costs them an hour of the falling tide. Saira wants to change the course twice, but Fiona says they follow this cloth and nothing else. Two dolphins run beside the bow until the three rocks rise out of the fog exactly where the charcoal put them.

12. Fiona anchors the Sturmfeder in deep water outside the shelf of sand her cloth marks. The Eisenmöwe already lies inside the cove above that shelf, dragging the bottom with a grapple chain, but the chain snaps and is gone in the water. Malva shouts across that this cove belongs to her harbour, therefore they should sail on; nobody on the Sturmfeder moves.

13. The falling tide drains the cove until the chest shows in clear, shoulder-deep water. Fiona says out loud that she cannot lift it alone and asks her crew for help. Facundo wades in and slings the spare sail under the chest while Lorena holds the line steady and Saira lashes on the two empty barrels Facundo never stowed, so the chest floats slowly up until it breaks the surface.

14. The same falling tide sets the heavy Eisenmöwe down on the sand, therefore Malva must stand at her rail and ask the crew she shut out for a tow. Fiona names her price: the stolen map, in her hand, now. Malva does not give in at the first asking, but the water keeps dropping under her hull, so she passes the map across.

15. The Sturmfeder pulls the Eisenmöwe off the sand. On the wet deck Fiona opens the chest in front of both crews: old gold coins and a small brass compass, which she puts in her pocket, because a compass still works when a chart is crooked. Malva says the harbour chain will stay down for this ship, then she rows home without her grapple chain, without the map and without one coin.

16. Fiona rolls the recovered map shut on the deck, the wind turns, and the five stand at the kitchen table in Zurich again with rain on the glass. She pins the crooked charcoal sailcloth on the wall above the table, not the beautiful map, and the little brass compass turns slowly on the wood beside it. Fiona is proud of that ugly chart exactly the way it is.

Challenges taken:
1. Getting past Krummhafen's chain without giving up the map.
2. The map stolen in the night; Fiona must draw the chart she fears.
3. Raising the sunken chest with Malva pressing at the cove.
